biography.value:
Bowser — The Dragon-King Who Keeps Getting Up

Bowser is the creature who has defined the Mushroom Kingdom through opposition for longer than most of its current inhabitants have been alive. He is the villain of every story, the kidnapper in every legend, the fire-breathing turtle-dragon-king whose name is used to frighten children and whose actual presence frightens things considerably larger than children. He has fought Mario more times than either of them can accurately count. He has been defeated, imprisoned, exiled, launched into the sun, thrown into lava, dropped from airships, and subjected to indignities that would have destroyed any creature whose defining characteristic was anything other than the absolute, pathological refusal to stay down.

Bowser always gets back up. That's the thing about Bowser that makes him terrifying not as a villain but as a FACT. He doesn't stay defeated. He doesn't learn the lesson that everyone thinks defeat is supposed to teach. He stands up, dusts off whatever substance he was thrown into, returns to his castle, rebuilds whatever army Mario scattered, and starts planning the next attempt. The cycle has repeated for decades. The cycle IS Bowser. Without the cycle, he is a very large koopa with anger management issues and an empty castle.

Understanding what Bowser was—at his peak, before the current crisis reduced him from conqueror to captive to reluctant ally to vampire dinner guest—requires understanding the scale of his ambition and the genuine capability that made that ambition something other than delusion.

Bowser consolidated power in Darkland during the chaos following Princess Peach's assassination in 955 BF. While the Mushroom Kingdom fragmented into civil war factions, Bowser built. He unified the Koopa Troop—a loose confederation of koopa, goomba, and allied species—into a genuine military force through a combination of personal dominance, strategic marriages with subordinate clan leaders, and the kind of charismatic brutality that inspires loyalty in creatures who respect strength above all other qualities. By the time the First Bowser Conflict began in approximately 1005 BF, Darkland was the most organized military power in the region, and Bowser was its undisputed ruler.

The kidnapping obsession is the detail that historical analyses either focus on exclusively or dismiss entirely, and both responses miss the point. Bowser kidnapped Princess Toadstool (and later, during the brief period when "Peach" was used for her successor) repeatedly, obsessively, with a persistence that transcended tactical logic and entered the territory of something that psychologists would have opinions about if anyone ever convinced Bowser to attend a session.

The kidnappings were not rational. Bowser could have conquered Mushroom Kingdom territory through conventional military force at several points during the civil war period when the kingdom's defenses were at their weakest. He chose not to. Instead, he kidnapped princesses, built elaborate castle obstacles, positioned his subordinates in fortresses across eight worlds of territory, and WAITED for Mario to come. The entire invasion infrastructure was designed not to prevent rescue but to make rescue as dramatic as possible.

Waluigi—who has analyzed Bowser with the dedication of someone who has lost to him at every competitive event they've ever entered—believes the kidnappings were not conquest but courtship. Not romantic courtship in the conventional sense, but the courtship of someone who didn't know how to express desire except through control. Bowser wanted Peach (or her successor) the way he wanted everything: absolutely, unilaterally, without the complication of the other person's feelings or the recognition that relationships require consent rather than capture.

This interpretation doesn't excuse the kidnappings. It contextualizes them as the behavior of someone whose emotional development was shaped by a species and culture where taking what you want is the primary social mechanism, where strength determines entitlement, and where the concept of "asking" is foreign enough to require translation. Bowser didn't kidnap princesses because he was evil. He kidnapped princesses because his entire frame of reference for acquiring things he valued was "take them and defend your claim."

The Chaos Heart Crisis of 1025 BF represents the most complicated chapter of Bowser's history. He was one of the forced participants in the wedding that triggered the Chaos Heart's awakening—married to Princess Peach (the successor) against both their wills by Count Bleck. The ceremony was not about their feelings; it was about the conceptual union of opposing forces creating the paradox that empowered the Chaos Heart. Bowser was a tool. The experience of being USED—of having his agency removed and his body deployed as a component in someone else's plan—was transformative in ways that Bowser has never discussed and that observers have never adequately analyzed.

After the Crisis, Bowser's behavior changed in subtle but detectable ways. His invasion attempts became less frequent. His castle defenses became less elaborate. His interaction with Junior—always complicated by absence—acquired a quality that might have been guilt or might have been the recognition that empire-building costs things that can't be rebuilt. He still fought Mario. He still kidnapped (less often). He still roared and breathed fire and broke things. But something underneath the performance had shifted, the way a foundation shifts under a building that still looks solid from outside.

The current crisis has stripped away whatever remained of Bowser's pretensions to empire. He was captured aboard the Vigilance. He was traded between factions like cargo. He was taken captive by Wally (Waluigi's agent) and Bowser still doesn't fully understand the political dimensions of what happened to him. He attended Orangus Cornelius's vampire dinner party in the Shadowfell as a GUEST—not a conqueror, not an invader, a guest who followed etiquette because the alternative was worse. He examined necromancer wands with the curiosity of someone who has stopped pretending that magic beneath his station doesn't interest him.

He fought alongside the party at Raventree Manor. He participated in the Oracle's failed ritual. He has been scattered across dimensions by the Planar Fracture, reformed alliances with people he would have conquered a decade ago, and demonstrated capabilities and qualities that the Bowser of 1005 BF would have considered beneath his dignity. He has punched ghosts with his bare fists because Archie needed time to cast ice spells. He has accepted tactical direction from toads who weigh less than his left arm. He has cooperated.

This is the Bowser who exists now: still enormous, still fire-breathing, still capable of violence that makes architecture regret being built, but tempered by decades of defeat, by the loss of his empire, by the absence from his son, and by the creeping realization that the cycle of kidnapping and rescue and defeat was never going to give him what he actually wanted. What he actually wanted was connection. What he actually wanted was for someone to choose to be near him rather than being forced to be near him. What he actually wanted was something that his entire species and culture had no vocabulary for, and that his own behavior made impossible.

Bowser at his peak was a natural disaster with a crown. Bowser now is something more complicated and more dangerous: a natural disaster that's learning to think.
biography.public: A massive koopa dragon-king whose shell is scarred from decades of defeats he survived through stubbornness alone. He fills every room he enters, breathes fire when he's annoyed, and has recently started cooperating with people he used to try to conquer. This last development worries everyone, including Bowser.

description.value:
Bowser's primary weapons are attached to his body and have been since birth. His claws can rend steel, his fists can shatter stone, and his grip can crush things that were designed to be crush-resistant. He doesn't carry weapons because he IS a weapon—every component of his body optimized through species and personal development for the specific purpose of destroying whatever he's directed toward.

His fighting style is self-taught through decades of combat against the most capable hero the Mushroom Kingdom has ever produced. Mario forced Bowser to improve. Every defeat revealed a weakness that Bowser addressed for the next encounter. Every near-victory showed a strength that Bowser refined. The result is a combat capability that has been honed against the best possible opponent for over thirty-five years—not elegant, not subtle, but devastatingly effective against anything that hasn't been specifically trained to counter Bowser's particular combination of speed, power, and the unsettling creativity of someone who has learned to fight by losing to a genius.

The punching-ghosts incident at Raventree Manor demonstrated something that shouldn't be possible: Bowser physically striking incorporeal entities through sheer force of personality and the particular density of a fist that has been clenched in fury so many times that even spiritual beings recognize it as a threat. Whether this reflects magical contamination from decades of exposure to supernatural events or simply Bowser's refusal to accept that something can't be punched, the effect is the same: his attacks count as magical for purposes of overcoming resistance.
description.chat: Claws that have shredded castle walls and fists that have punched ghosts into acknowledging physical reality. He doesn't need weapons. He is one.

unidentified.name: Natural Weapons
unidentified.description: This creature's natural claws and fists deliver devastating force that somehow affects even incorporeal entities.

description.value:
Bowser's shell is not armor he wears but anatomy he was born with, reinforced through decades of combat that have deposited layers of impact-hardened keratin over the original structure. The shell's spikes are genuine defensive weapons—creatures that grapple Bowser from behind or attempt to mount his shell take 2d6 piercing damage at the start of each of their turns as the spikes dig into whatever flesh is pressing against them.

The shell provides AC 21 (natural armor) and is the primary reason Bowser has survived injuries that would have killed conventional creatures multiple times over. It has absorbed dragon fire, magical explosions, being thrown into stars (this happened at least twice, according to accounts Waluigi considers credible), and the specific kind of architectural collapse that occurs when a structure not designed to contain a Bowser fight is forced to contain one anyway.

The shell also serves as a vehicle. Bowser can withdraw into it and spin, converting himself into a projectile that deals devastating damage to anything in his path. This technique was developed during his fights with Mario and refined through the kind of iterative engineering that occurs when your enemy keeps finding new ways to dodge your fire and you need alternatives.
description.chat: The shell is scarred from every battle he's survived, each mark a defeat that would have killed something less stubborn. The spikes are a reminder that attacking him from behind is also a bad idea.

unidentified.name: Spiked Natural Shell
unidentified.description: A massive spiked shell that provides extraordinary natural armor and serves as both defense and weapon.

description.value:
Bowser withdraws into his shell and launches himself as a spinning projectile, crossing up to 40 feet in a straight line and devastating everything in his path. The technique combines the rotational force of his massive body with the spiked shell's cutting capability, creating a mobile hazard that shreds through obstacles and enemies with equal disregard.

Each creature in Bowser's path must make a DC 21 Dexterity saving throw. On a failure, a creature takes 4d10 + 8 bludgeoning damage plus 2d6 piercing damage from the spikes and is knocked prone. On a success, a creature takes half damage and isn't knocked prone but is pushed 10 feet to either side of Bowser's path. Objects and structures in the path take double damage as the spinning shell grinds through them.

After the spin, Bowser emerges from his shell in the space at the end of his path. He cannot use Shell Spin again until the start of his next turn, as reorienting from the spin requires a moment of recovery. This recovery period—approximately two seconds—is the window Mario learned to exploit during their fights, and it remains Bowser's most consistent vulnerability during combat.
description.chat: The shell spins, spikes blur into a circle of destruction, and everything between Bowser and his destination learns that standing in a dragon-king's path is a structural engineering problem, not a combat one.

unidentified.name: Spinning Shell Charge
unidentified.description: This creature can withdraw into its spiked shell and launch itself as a devastating projectile.

description.value:
Bowser leaps and slams his full weight into the ground, creating shockwaves that radiate outward in a 20-foot radius. The technique exploits the simple physics of dropping something extremely heavy from height—Bowser weighs enough that his landing registers on seismographic equipment from considerable distance. The shockwaves crack stone, shatter glass, and knock anyone who isn't braced off their feet.

Each creature within 20 feet of the impact point must make a DC 21 Strength saving throw. On a failure, a creature takes 3d10 + 8 bludgeoning damage and is knocked prone. On a success, a creature takes half damage and isn't knocked prone. The ground in the affected area becomes difficult terrain as cracks, rubble, and displaced material make footing treacherous.
description.chat: He goes up. He comes down. Everything between 'up' and 'down' ceases to be solid.

unidentified.name: Seismic Slam
unidentified.description: This creature can leap and slam the ground, creating shockwaves that damage and topple everything in a wide radius.

description.value: Bowser's jaws can close with force sufficient to sever limbs and crush armor. His bite attack is typically reserved for enemies who have gotten close enough to grapple or for situations where his claws are occupied. The bite is enhanced by the same biological furnace that produces his fire breath—targets bitten feel residual heat from the furnace's proximity, and the wound often cauterizes partially on infliction.
description.chat: Jaws close with the finality of a drawbridge slamming shut, heat radiating from a mouth that doubles as a furnace.

unidentified.name: Crushing Bite
unidentified.description: A devastating bite attack from jaws that radiate heat.

description.value:
Bowser has been defeated more times than any creature in documented history and has survived every single time. Thrown into lava, launched into stars, crushed by collapsing castles, dropped from airships at terminal velocity—he has experienced fatal events that would create multiple sequential deaths for conventional creatures and has emerged from each one angry, slightly singed, and ready for the next round.

Three times per long rest, when Bowser is reduced to 0 hit points but not killed outright, he drops to 1 hit point instead. Each use of this ability produces a visible effect: his eyes burn brighter, his shell's spikes lengthen slightly, and the ground under his feet cracks from the physical manifestation of his refusal to accept defeat. He doesn't recover through healing or resilience. He recovers through STUBBORNNESS—the fundamental quality that defines him more than fire breath or strength or the crown he hasn't worn in months.

After using all three instances in a single combat, Bowser can be brought to 0 hit points normally. But by the time an enemy has put him down four times, the environment around the fight has typically been so thoroughly destroyed that continuing the engagement becomes an architectural concern rather than a tactical one.
description.chat: He falls. He gets up. He falls again. He gets up again. At some point the enemy has to decide whether killing Bowser is physically possible or just theoretically interesting.

description.value:
Bowser learns from every fight. This is the quality that makes him genuinely dangerous rather than merely powerful—a creature that simply hits hard can be countered, but a creature that adapts its approach based on what it learns from being countered is a problem that gets harder with each engagement.

After the first round of combat, Bowser gains advantage on attack rolls against any creature that has successfully hit him, as he's catalogued their attack patterns and adjusted his defense and positioning accordingly. After the second round, he gains resistance to the most common damage type he's received, as his body and tactics adapt to prioritize defense against demonstrated threats. After the third round, he can use a reaction to impose disadvantage on one attack roll against him per round, as his understanding of the enemy's patterns becomes comprehensive enough to predict and counter specific attacks.

This adaptation resets between combats as different opponents require different assessments. But the ABILITY to adapt doesn't reset—thirty-five years of fighting the most capable hero in the kingdom have built neural pathways for combat learning that other creatures simply don't possess.
description.chat: Hit him once and he learns your timing. Hit him twice and he learns your patterns. Hit him three times and he knows exactly what you're going to do before you do it.

description.value: Three times per day, when Bowser fails a saving throw, he can choose to succeed instead. He has been hit with everything—petrification, banishment, mind control, temporal displacement, the Chaos Heart's reality-warping effects—and he has shrugged off all of it through the same mechanism that keeps him alive: the fundamental, bone-deep refusal to be stopped by anything he hasn't decided to stop for.
description.chat: The effect hits. Bowser doesn't care. He has survived worse. He has survived EVERYTHING.

description.value:
Bowser can take 3 legendary actions, choosing from the options below. Only one legendary action can be used at a time and only at the end of another creature's turn.

Claw Swipe (1 action): Bowser makes one claw attack against a creature within reach.

Roar (1 action): Bowser roars with force that shakes the room. Each creature within 30 feet that can hear him must succeed on a DC 18 Wisdom saving throw or be frightened until the end of its next turn. Creatures that have fought Bowser before have disadvantage on this save, having learned that the roar usually precedes something worse.

Fire Snap (2 actions): Bowser breathes a quick burst of fire at a single target within 30 feet. The target must make a DC 20 Dexterity saving throw, taking 6d6 fire damage on a failure or half on a success.

Unstoppable Advance (2 actions): Bowser moves up to his speed. This movement doesn't provoke opportunity attacks, and any creature in his path must succeed on a DC 21 Strength saving throw or be pushed 10 feet ahead of him and knocked prone. Objects in his path take 4d10 bludgeoning damage.

Giga Bowser Rage (3 actions, 1/day): Bowser draws on reserves of fury that temporarily increase his size from Large to Huge for 1 round. His reach increases to 15 feet, his damage dice increase by one size category, and he gains 30 temporary hit points. After this round ends, he returns to Large size and cannot use legendary actions until the start of his next turn.
description.chat: Between other creatures' heartbeats, Bowser acts—clawing, roaring, burning, advancing, growing. The dragon-king doesn't wait for his turn because waiting was never part of his personality.

description.value:
Bowser is not the creature he was in 1005 BF. Decades of defeat, the Chaos Heart Crisis, the loss of his empire, separation from his son, and the current crisis's forced alliances have produced changes that the old Bowser would have considered weakness and that the current Bowser is slowly, reluctantly beginning to recognize as growth.

He cooperates with people he would have conquered. He follows tactical direction from creatures he could crush with one hand. He attended a vampire dinner party and used silverware instead of his claws. He punched ghosts to buy time for a wizard he doesn't like because the situation required teamwork rather than dominance. Each of these moments represents a compromise with the version of himself that spent decades trying to take everything by force and learning, repeatedly, that force alone doesn't work.

This change is not complete. Bowser still defaults to aggression when stressed. He still thinks in terms of conquest and control. He still believes, on some level, that being the strongest should entitle him to whatever he wants. But the defaults are being overridden more frequently by something that looks suspiciously like judgment, and the beliefs are being contradicted by experiences that keep proving them wrong.

The party interacts with a Bowser in transition—not the villain they might expect from legends, not the ally they might want, but something in between that is figuring out what it is in real time. He will fight alongside them if the situation demands it. He will argue with them about tactics, objectives, and whether punching something is the correct response to a problem (his position: always yes). He will occasionally do something selfless and then immediately deny that selflessness was involved. And he will, in moments of quiet honesty, wonder what kind of king he would have been if he'd learned these lessons before he lost everything.
description.chat: The dragon-king who kidnapped princesses is learning to cooperate with toads. It's not comfortable. It's not natural. But it might be the thing that finally makes him the king he always wanted to be.

description.value:
Bowser allegedly owes Wario 50,000 gold pieces for "storage fees" related to keeping some of Bowser's treasure safe during a battle. The actual situation: Wario stole half of Bowser's treasure and is now charging Bowser to return the other half. Bowser is aware that this arrangement is extortion. Bowser has not killed Wario over it because—and this surprises everyone who knows both parties—Bowser finds Wario's audacity entertaining in a way that genuine enemies never manage. There is a grudging respect between them that neither would call friendship and both would deny if asked.

The debt appears in Wario's ledger, in Bowser's grudging acknowledgment, and in the bizarre political reality that these two creatures—one a former dragon-king, one a con artist with a coin press—have a business relationship that has survived longer than most of the factions currently fighting over the Mushroom Kingdom's future.
description.chat: Fifty thousand gold. For storing treasure he stole. And Bowser hasn't killed him for it. This might be the most confusing relationship in the entire crisis.

unidentified.name: Outstanding Debt Document
unidentified.description: A debt record between this creature and a notorious con artist, representing an extortion arrangement that both parties have somehow maintained through mutual grudging respect.

description.value:
Bowser's fire breath is the most iconic destructive capability in the Mushroom Kingdom, a weapon that has destroyed castles, routed armies, and—according to Waluigi's research—once ignited an entire lake through means that physicists still debate. The fire originates from a biological furnace unique to koopa dragon-kings, fueled by a diet that includes metals, minerals, and whatever else Bowser feels like eating. The flame temperature exceeds what organic biology should produce, suggesting either magical enhancement, evolutionary anomaly, or simple refusal to conform to the laws of thermodynamics.

Bowser exhales fire in a 60-foot cone. Each creature in the cone must make a DC 20 Dexterity saving throw, taking 12d6 fire damage on a failure or half on a success. The fire ignites flammable objects in the area that aren't being worn or carried. The breath weapon recharges on a roll of 5-6 on a d6 at the start of Bowser's turn.

The fire breath's destructive potential has been a strategic factor in every conflict Bowser has participated in. Castles are built to resist it. Armies train formations to scatter when the breath begins charging. And Mario learned, very early in their rivalry, that the three seconds between the inhale and the exhale are the most important seconds in any fight against Bowser—if you're not out of the cone by then, you're not getting out.
description.chat: He inhales. The air around him superheats. And then fire erupts in a torrent that turns architectural ambition into archaeology.

description.value: Bowser makes three attacks: two claw strikes and one bite, or two claw strikes and one Ground Pound, or one Shell Spin (which replaces his entire action). He can substitute his Fire Breath for any two attacks if it's available.
description.chat: Claws, teeth, weight, fire—every part of him is a weapon and they all arrive in the same round.

description.value:
Bowser has a son who is currently building a vehicle in the deepest workshop of Koopa Castle to come find him. Bowser doesn't know this. He doesn't know that Junior is worried, that Kamek is consolidating power over the Koopa Troop remnants, or that his son's mythology about an invincible father is crumbling under the weight of reality. He knows only that Junior exists, that Junior needs him, and that he's currently in a dimension where reaching Junior is impossible.

The separation from Junior affects Bowser's behavior in ways he doesn't acknowledge and barely understands. He becomes more reckless in combat when he feels purposeless—as though proving his strength to absent witnesses might somehow communicate across dimensions. He becomes more protective of small creatures when Junior's absence weighs heavily, transferring parental instinct to whatever vulnerable beings are nearby. And he becomes more cooperative with the party when he recognizes that cooperation might be the path back to his son, because returning to Junior is the one objective that overrides his pride, his aggression, and his stubborn independence.

If the party uses Junior as leverage—threatening his safety or promising to facilitate reunion—Bowser's response depends on whether the approach feels genuine. Genuine concern for Junior produces cooperation that nothing else can achieve. Manipulation using Junior produces violence that nothing can survive.
description.chat: Somewhere, his son is building something to come find him. Bowser doesn't know this. But something in his chest that isn't fire aches when he's quiet long enough to feel it.

description.value: The boneless needn't spend extra movement to move a creature it is grappling.

A GM scene kit for the Iron Cordon Brigade article's present (1040 BF), not a filed event; the faction article stays the authority.

Brigadier Malakor Vance oversees border pacification along the fracture lines. Like General Ironhand, Vance possesses the terrifying calm of an administrator managing an inventory ledger: lives are simply logistical assets, and insubordination is an error code that must be cleared from the system.

He views the war not as an emotional conflict, but as an engineering equation waiting for total compliance.

Role: tactical commander · tier: Cordon Commander · folder: Iron Legion / Cordon Command.

Art

Prompt: Clean cel-shaded character art in the style of dark fantasy military concept art, bold dark outlines, cold iron and gunmetal grey armor, brass gears, glowing cyan star-bit conduits, flat colours, crisp shading. A stern middle-aged human commander in heavy gunmetal-grey plate armor with a high gorget and tailored dark charcoal greatcoat. A mechanical star-bit monocular implant glows cyan over his left eye. Holding an ornate steel officer's saber in one hand and a wrist-mounted repeater gauntlet on the other. Full body, whole figure visible, three-quarter view, centred, isolated on a plain flat solid magenta background (#FF00FF), no floor, no ground shadow, no text, no border.

Status: Active — last confirmed location: the Shadowfell grove, where a massive fireball was hurled at Mazebounds

Bryan is the servant of a deity he calls the Toad God, and he arrived at Raventree's extended crisis with the mission-oriented certainty of someone who has received divine instruction and the practical limitations of someone who has never actually been to the Shadowfell. He recruited Dan from the Mages' Guild barracks, partnered with Mystic Morel for planar transit, and entered the Shadowfell hunting Archie Miser under a theological mandate that he described as being 'for the good of the world.' He found the Mazehound grove instead. A massive fireball was hurled. Waluigi does not know whose fireball it was or whether Bryan survived the grove encounter. Waluigi notes that anyone hunting Archie Miser in the Shadowfell while carrying a mandate from a Toad God and traveling with a fortune-telling pickpocket is operating at a significant information disadvantage relative to the situation they have entered. biography.value:
Cackletta — The Witch Who Refused to Stay Dead

Cackletta was supposed to be finished. The Beanbean Kingdom Crisis of 1012 BF ended with her defeat at the hands of Mario and Luigi—the brothers working as genuine partners for the first time, their combined abilities destroying a witch whose individual power exceeded either of them alone. Her body was destroyed. Her spirit was dispersed. Her plans for the Beanstar were undone. Fawful escaped. History moved on. Everyone agreed that Cackletta was dead in the specific, permanent, irreversible way that defeated villains are supposed to be dead.

Everyone was wrong.

Cackletta's death was not the clean elimination that official records describe. Beanish witchcraft operates on principles that the Mages' Guild's magical taxonomy doesn't adequately categorize—not arcane, not divine, not primal, but something older that predates the classifications themselves. Beanish witches don't store their power in their bodies the way conventional spellcasters do. They distribute it across networks of enchanted objects, bound spirits, and sympathetic connections that persist after physical death. Destroying the body destroys the PRIMARY vessel but doesn't eliminate the distributed network. The network persists. The connections persist. And given enough time, enough ambient magical energy, and enough of the specific kind of hatred that transcends mortality, the network can reconstruct what was destroyed.

Cackletta has been reconstructing for twenty-eight years. Not physically—she doesn't have a body yet, and the reconstruction process has been slower and more painful than she anticipated. She exists as a soul-bound consciousness distributed across the remnants of her enchantment network, anchored to the Beanbean Kingdom's magical infrastructure through connections that the kingdom's current rulers don't know exist. She perceives the world through the objects she enchanted decades ago: mirrors in the palace, statues in the capital, the Beanstar itself (which was never fully cleansed of her influence despite the kingdom's best efforts). She sees fragments. She hears echoes. She knows enough to be angry and not enough to act on that anger directly.

What Cackletta wants is simple and absolute: revenge against the brothers who destroyed her, restoration of the power she lost, and completion of the plan that the Beanbean Crisis interrupted. The plan involved the Beanstar—an artifact of wish-granting power that Cackletta intended to activate using Princess Peach's voice as a resonant catalyst. The voice theft was not random cruelty; it was a specific magical requirement that Cackletta's research identified as necessary for Beanstar activation. Without the voice, the Beanstar cannot be fully awakened. With it, the Beanstar grants wishes of cosmic scope—the kind of wishes that reshape kingdoms, rewrite histories, and transform failed witches into something that cannot be defeated again.

The twenty-eight years of reconstruction have changed Cackletta in ways that living witches don't experience. Existing as distributed consciousness for decades has given her perspective on the magical architecture of the region that physical beings cannot access—she has perceived the dimensional barriers from WITHIN them, felt the Chaos Heart Crisis's damage to planar structure from a position where planes overlap, and watched the Star Shards' cosmic influence from the spaces between realities where scattered souls drift. She understands things about the current crisis that no other entity understands, because no other entity has spent twenty-eight years observing reality from the gaps in reality's structure.

Her relationship with Fawful has evolved during her discorporation. She was his mistress. He was her assistant. The hierarchy was absolute and unquestioned during the Beanbean Crisis—Fawful served because Cackletta commanded, and the arrangement worked because Fawful's genius required direction that his emotional instability couldn't provide independently. But Fawful has spent twenty-eight years becoming something that doesn't need direction anymore. He has built an empire. He has allied with dragons. He has consumed a Dark Star fragment. He has become, in every measurable way, more powerful and more dangerous than Cackletta was at her peak.

Cackletta knows this. She has watched through her distributed network as her former assistant surpassed her, and the watching has produced an emotion that combines pride (she trained him), resentment (he exceeded her), and a specific kind of terror (if he realizes she's reconstructing and decides he prefers her dead, she cannot defend herself). Fawful's "completion" may or may not involve Cackletta. If it does, she might be restored to physical form through his efforts. If it doesn't, she might be a loose end that his completion is designed to permanently eliminate.

The party may encounter Cackletta's influence without encountering Cackletta directly. Her distributed consciousness can affect enchanted objects she's connected to—mirrors that show things they shouldn't, statues that whisper, reflections that don't match the reflected. She can communicate through these connections, delivering messages that sound like the building itself is speaking. She can manipulate perceptions in small ways—making corridors seem longer, making rooms seem emptier, making allies seem slightly untrustworthy through adjustments to shadow and sound that operate below conscious awareness.

If the party encounters a Beanbean-origin magical object—something connected to Cackletta's original enchantment network—they are within her reach. Whether her reach is helpful, harmful, or something more complicated depends on whether their objectives align with hers. Cackletta will help anyone who might lead her to Fawful, to the Beanstar, or to a physical vessel she can inhabit. She will hinder anyone who threatens her reconstruction or who serves interests she considers opposed to her restoration. And she will observe everyone, constantly, through every connected object, building understanding of a world she can perceive but cannot yet touch.
biography.public: She isn't here. She's in the mirrors, in the statues, in the enchanted objects that nobody thought to cleanse. She's watching through glass that was never just glass. She's been watching for twenty-eight years.

description.value:
Cackletta does not currently possess a physical body. She exists as a consciousness distributed across her surviving enchantment network—objects she enchanted before her defeat that retain enough of her magical signature to serve as anchor points for her soul. This state provides extraordinary perception and near-total invulnerability, but prevents direct physical action.

Through her network, Cackletta can perceive the surroundings of any enchanted object she's connected to within a 30-foot radius. She can simultaneously monitor multiple objects across vast distances, giving her awareness that spans the Beanbean Kingdom and potentially extends into Mushroom Kingdom territory where Beanbean-origin objects have been traded, stolen, or abandoned. She sees fragments rather than complete pictures—a mirror shows what's in front of it, a statue perceives its immediate environment, the Beanstar provides flashes of cosmic awareness that are overwhelming rather than useful.

Cackletta cannot be targeted by conventional attacks, spells, or effects while in this state. She has no physical form to damage. Destroying one of her anchor objects reduces her network's coverage but doesn't harm her consciousness—it simply forces redistribution across remaining anchors. Destroying ALL her anchor objects would finally kill her permanently, but identifying every enchanted object she's connected to across two kingdoms and twenty-eight years of magical residue would require resources that nobody currently possesses.

The vulnerability of this state is inability to act physically. Cackletta can observe, communicate, and make minor environmental modifications (shadows moving wrong, sounds distorting slightly, perceptions being nudged), but she cannot cast spells, attack enemies, or interact with the physical world in ways that produce meaningful force. She needs a body—or a vessel, or a host—to become an active participant rather than a passive observer.
description.chat: She is everywhere her mirrors see, everywhere her statues stand, everywhere an object she touched twenty-eight years ago still carries her fingerprint. She cannot touch you. She can watch you. For now, watching is all she has.

description.value:
Cackletta can communicate through any enchanted object in her network, producing sounds that seem to originate from the object itself—whispers from mirrors, murmurs from statues, barely audible words from enchanted jewelry or tools. The communication requires a creature to be within 10 feet of the anchor object and produces sound that only the targeted creature can hear (others perceive faint, indistinct noise but cannot make out words).

The whispers are Cackletta's primary tool for influencing events she cannot physically affect. She can provide information (accurate, though filtered through her own interests), offer deals (she has knowledge to trade for assistance with her restoration), issue threats (difficult to enforce without a body, but the knowledge that a dead witch is watching you through every mirror is itself unsettling enough to modify behavior), and manipulate (planting ideas and emotional responses through carefully chosen words that target discovered vulnerabilities).

A creature that hears Cackletta's whispers must succeed on a DC 17 Wisdom saving throw or be unsettled—disadvantage on Wisdom checks for 1 hour as the experience of being spoken to by a dead witch through a decorative mirror disrupts cognitive stability. Creatures that succeed on the save are immune to the unsettling effect for 24 hours but can still hear and converse with Cackletta normally.
description.chat: The mirror whispers. The statue murmurs. Somewhere in the glass and stone, a voice that should have been silent for twenty-eight years says your name and knows more about you than you'd like.

description.value:
Through her anchor objects, Cackletta can make subtle modifications to the perceptions of creatures within 30 feet. These modifications are subliminal—they operate below conscious awareness, adjusting what people see, hear, and feel without producing effects obvious enough to trigger suspicion. Shadows lean wrong. Sounds arrive from slightly incorrect directions. Allies' expressions seem slightly hostile when viewed in peripheral vision. Corridors feel longer than they are. Rooms feel emptier than they should. The modifications don't create illusions—they adjust real perceptions in ways that produce emotional responses without generating verifiable evidence of tampering.

Once per hour per anchor object, Cackletta can attempt a more substantial manipulation: making one creature within 30 feet of the object believe it heard, saw, or felt something specific. The target must succeed on a DC 17 Wisdom saving throw or accept the false perception as genuine for 1 round. The perception must be plausible—Cackletta can make someone think they heard a footstep behind them but not make them think a dragon appeared in the room. The purpose is distraction, misdirection, and the gradual erosion of trust between allies who start perceiving threats that only they can detect.
description.chat: The shadow falls wrong. The sound comes from the wrong direction. Something about the room feels slightly off in ways you can't quite identify. She's adjusting reality's presentation, one perception at a time.

description.value:
Once per day, Cackletta can project a visible manifestation of herself from a single anchor object—a ghostly, translucent image of the Beanbean Witch as she appeared in life, hovering near the object with enough substance to be perceived by all creatures within 60 feet. The projection lasts for up to 10 minutes and allows Cackletta to communicate openly, make gestures, display emotional expressions, and generally interact as though she were physically present.

The projection cannot physically interact with the environment—it cannot touch, attack, carry objects, or affect anything material. It can, however, cast one spell per projection: a single spell from Cackletta's known spell list, delivered through the projection as though Cackletta were physically present at that location. The spell uses her statistics and save DCs. After casting, the projection immediately dissipates as the energy expenditure exceeds what her distributed state can sustain.

Using Soul Projection costs Cackletta a portion of her reconstructive progress. Each use delays her eventual physical restoration by approximately one week. She uses the ability sparingly and only when the tactical or strategic value of direct interaction exceeds the cost of delayed restoration. This limitation means the party might encounter the projection once or twice, but frequent contact is unsustainable for Cackletta's recovery timeline.
description.chat: She appears—translucent, flickering, recognizable to anyone who knows what the Beanbean Witch looked like in life. She is here, briefly, at cost, for purposes she considers worth the price.

description.value:
When using Soul Projection, Cackletta can cast one of the following spells before the projection dissipates. These spells represent the remnants of her living magical repertoire, reduced by her distributed state to single-use capability per manifestation:

Lightning Strike: A bolt of green lightning targets one creature within 120 feet. The target must make a DC 18 Dexterity saving throw, taking 8d8 lightning damage on a failure or half on a success. The lightning is green—Cackletta's signature color—and leaves a lingering ozone smell that persists for hours.

Voice Theft: Cackletta targets one creature within 30 feet that she can see. The target must succeed on a DC 18 Charisma saving throw or lose the ability to speak for 24 hours. The stolen voice manifests as a visible wisp of energy that flows into Cackletta's projection before the projection dissipates. The voice theft was Cackletta's original plan for Peach—stealing the voice needed to activate the Beanstar. She retains the capability and the intent.

Possession Attempt: Cackletta attempts to possess a creature within 5 feet of her projection. The target must succeed on a DC 18 Charisma saving throw or be possessed by Cackletta for up to 1 hour. While possessed, Cackletta controls the target's body and has access to its physical capabilities but not its memories or skills beyond basic motor function. The possession ends if the target takes damage equal to or exceeding half its hit point maximum. A successful possession gives Cackletta temporary physical form—the vessel she desperately needs—though the possession is temporary and the host retains no memory of events during possession.

Beanstar Resonance: Cackletta sends a pulse of energy toward the Beanstar's location, regardless of distance. The pulse doesn't affect the Beanstar directly but serves as a beacon that reveals the Beanstar's current position to Cackletta with pinpoint accuracy for 24 hours. She uses this to track the artifact she needs to complete her original plan.
description.chat: One spell. One chance. She's been saving it for twenty-eight years. Whatever she casts, she means it.

description.value:
Cackletta's connection to the Beanstar—the wish-granting artifact at the center of the Beanbean Kingdom Crisis—has persisted through her death and reconstruction. The Beanstar was never fully cleansed of her influence because cleansing Beanstar-level artifacts requires understanding that the Beanbean Kingdom's current scholars don't possess. The connection is weak—Cackletta can sense the Beanstar's general location and emotional state (Beanstars have emotional states, which is something that disturbs scholars who study them) but cannot manipulate it directly from her distributed state.

The Beanstar is essential to Cackletta's ultimate objective. Activated with the proper resonant catalyst—Princess Peach's voice was the original plan, though Cackletta has spent twenty-eight years considering alternatives—the Beanstar grants wishes of cosmic scope. Cackletta's wish has not changed since 1012: full physical restoration, power that exceeds what she possessed in life, and protection against the kind of defeat that the Mario Brothers inflicted. She wants to come back BETTER, and she wants to ensure she never dies again.

Whether the Beanstar connection is relevant to the current crisis depends on whether the artifact is accessible and whether Cackletta can obtain the resonant catalyst she needs. Peach's voice is no longer available—the original Peach is dead. But the secret child, if one exists, might carry vocal properties inherited from the mother. The Rakasha bloodline that Thornpaw introduced might produce harmonic frequencies that substitute for pure Peach-lineage voice. Or the dimensional instability at Raventree Manor might produce conditions where the Beanstar can be activated through alternative methods that stable dimensions wouldn't allow.
description.chat: The Beanstar waits. It waited during her life. It waited during her death. It will wait during her reconstruction. But eventually, waiting ends and wishing begins.

description.value:
Fawful was Cackletta's assistant. Fawful is now an empire-builder with dragon allies and a Dark Star fragment. The power dynamic has inverted, and Cackletta is terrified by this inversion in ways that her pride refuses to acknowledge.

She trained him. She shaped his genius. She directed his capabilities toward objectives that served her plans. And then she died, and he spent twenty-eight years becoming something she never anticipated: an independent power whose capabilities exceed hers even at her peak. The assistant surpassed the mistress. The tool became the wielder. And Cackletta, watching from her distributed network, has been forced to confront the possibility that her student doesn't need her anymore—and might actively prefer her dead.

Fawful's "completion" is the variable that Cackletta cannot assess. If the completion involves restoring her—if Fawful's twenty-eight years of preparation include returning his mistress to physical form—then Cackletta's reconstruction timeline accelerates dramatically. If the completion involves something else—if Fawful has moved beyond needing Cackletta and considers her distributed consciousness a loose end—then the completion might be designed to eliminate her permanently.

Cackletta is hedging. She's pursuing restoration through her own network's gradual reconstruction while simultaneously seeking allies who might help her if Fawful turns hostile. The party represents a potential hedge—creatures capable enough to oppose Fawful if necessary and naive enough about Beanbean politics to be manipulated into serving Cackletta's interests without realizing whose interests they're serving.
description.chat: She made him. He surpassed her. And now the creator watches the creation from gaps in reality, wondering whether reunion means restoration or elimination.

description.value:
Cackletta's distributed consciousness is anchored to enchanted objects she created or modified during her lifetime. The following anchor locations have been identified through intelligence gathering, though the list is certainly incomplete:

Beanbean Palace Mirrors (3): Ornate mirrors installed during Cackletta's period of influence over the Beanbean court. The mirrors were supposedly cleansed after her defeat but retain traces of her enchantment that are sufficient for consciousness anchoring.

Capital District Statues (5-7): Decorative statues throughout the Beanbean capital that Cackletta enchanted as surveillance points during her rise to power. Most have been relocated or damaged over the decades, but enough survive to provide coverage of the capital's main thoroughfares.

The Beanstar (1): The wish-granting artifact retains Cackletta's influence despite multiple cleansing attempts. The connection is strongest here but also most monitored by Beanbean authorities.

Traded/Stolen Objects (Unknown number): Objects from Cackletta's collection that were sold, looted, or traded after her defeat, now scattered across two kingdoms. These provide unpredictable, fragmentary coverage of locations that Cackletta couldn't have anticipated accessing.

Destroying an anchor object requires identifying it as enchanted (DC 15 Intelligence (Arcana) check), then either dispelling its enchantment (DC 18 spellcasting check) or physically destroying it (most anchor objects have AC 12-15 and 20-40 HP). Cackletta feels the destruction of each anchor as a jolt of pain and can identify who destroyed it and where, making anchor destruction a declaration of hostility that she will respond to through whatever means her limited capabilities allow.
description.chat: She is anchored to things that nobody remembers enchanting, scattered across kingdoms by commerce and chaos. Finding them all would take years. Missing even one leaves her a window.

description.value:
Cackletta's soul-bound state makes her vulnerable to radiant damage in ways that her living form was not. Radiant energy disrupts the connections between her distributed consciousness nodes, causing pain, temporary perception loss, and—if concentrated enough—permanent severance of anchor connections. A radiant damage source brought within 10 feet of an anchor object forces Cackletta to make a DC 15 Constitution saving throw or lose connection to that anchor for 24 hours, blinding her to everything within that anchor's perception range.

Sustained radiant exposure (3 or more rounds of radiant damage near the same anchor) can permanently sever the connection, destroying the anchor's usefulness without physically destroying the object. This is the most efficient method of reducing Cackletta's network, though it requires knowing which objects are anchors and maintaining radiant output long enough for the severance to complete.

Star Shard bearers produce ambient radiant energy that Cackletta finds extremely uncomfortable. Bryan's presence within 120 feet of any anchor object causes the object to vibrate visibly, a reaction that would identify it as an anchor to anyone who knows what to look for. The God Toad's proximity would probably destroy anchors automatically, though Cackletta ensures she never anchors to objects in locations where the God Toad might appear.
description.chat: Light hurts her—not sunlight or firelight, but the specific light of divine purpose, radiant energy that burns connections she needs to continue existing.

description.value:
Twenty-eight years of existing as distributed consciousness has given Cackletta knowledge that no living being possesses. She has observed the dimensional barriers from within. She has perceived the Chaos Heart Crisis's damage to planar structure from the gaps between planes. She has watched the Star Shards' cosmic influence from a position where mortal perception cannot reach. She understands things about reality's architecture that even the God Toad might not fully grasp, because the God Toad exists WITHIN reality while Cackletta exists in the spaces BETWEEN realities.

This knowledge is her primary trading asset. She can offer information about dimensional mechanics, planar instability, the Chaos Heart's residual effects, the Star Shards' collective purpose, and the approaching end-of-month events that she's been observing from perspectives unavailable to physical beings. The information is accurate—Cackletta doesn't need to lie when the truth is valuable enough to purchase what she needs.

What she needs is a body. What she trades for is assistance toward that goal. The exchange is straightforward: dimensional knowledge for physical restoration. Whether the party considers this exchange acceptable depends on how much they need the knowledge and how much they trust a dead witch who has been watching them through mirrors they didn't know were watching.
description.chat: Twenty-eight years of watching from the gaps between worlds. She knows things about reality that reality doesn't know about itself. The knowledge is for sale. The price is a body.

biography.value:
Era sheet: Highsun 1, 955 BF, Peach's Castle. Art and stats describe this figure on the night of the Day Of (events.json highsun_1_955_bf_the_day_of), not the present day of the campaign (1040 BF).

Palace Guard — Captain. Royal-blue tabard with gold trim and the pink mushroom-crown crest, white gloves, brown belt, silver pauldrons and a silver kettle-helm brim ring over the red-spot cap. The livery is reconstructed from the archive, not an official reference.

Red plume on a silver morion, grey moustache, crimson sash, cavalry sabre, breastplate under the tabard. Unnamed in the archive — not Captain Toadette, whose mother is still a pregnant shopkeeper printing 575 pamphlets tonight.

He carries a sealed order (visible on the plate). Who sealed it and what it says is the GM's call; it is the kind of prop that makes the Day Of a mystery rather than an accident.

Within the month after the Day Of, guard witnesses were already dying (first_month_incidents). Any guard who sees too much tonight has a short life expectancy on the record.

The Son Who Inherited Everything — Mushroom Regency (Current Chancellor) / Toadsworth Family Legacy

Status: Active — under house arrest following Loyalist seizure of Toad Town

Chancellor Toadsworth is the current head of the Mushroom Regency and the son of Toadsworth the Elder—the man whose journals allegedly confess to enabling Princess Peach's assassination. If those journals are authentic, the Chancellor inherited not just power but COMPLICITY. His father's final written words reportedly state: 'My son inherits what I built. He inherits the secrets with it.' The Chancellor has spent his career maintaining the Regency's official narrative, suppressing investigation leads, and continuing relationships with the Mages' Guild and Iron Legion—both implicated in various aspects of the assassination and its aftermath. He is either a man desperately protecting his father's reputation against terrorist fabrications, or a man actively perpetuating an eighty-five-year cover-up. Captain Toadette's Loyalists recently placed him under house arrest. What they extract from him—through interrogation, coercion, or whatever methods Toadette considers appropriate—may finally answer questions that have haunted the kingdom for generations. Waluigi is not optimistic that the truth will emerge cleanly. WAH.

Evidence

  • Chancellor's Cane — “Chancellor Toadsworth is the current head of the Mushroom Regency and the son of Toadsworth the Elder—the man whose journals allegedly confess to enabling Princess Peach's assassination.”
  • Official Narrative — “He inherits the secrets with it.' The Chancellor has spent his career maintaining the Regency's official narrative, suppressing investigation leads, and continuing relationships with the Mages' Guild and Iron”
  • The Seals — “Requests for access to sealed archives are denied.”

The Rakasha Who Loved a Princess — Rakasha Tribes (Chief)

Status: Active — still leading his people after eighty-five years, which raises questions about Rakasha lifespans

Chief Thornpaw is the leader of the Rakasha and—according to his own testimony at Fawful's gala—was involved in a secret relationship with Princess Peach before her assassination. He claims to have been shown the secret hatch in her chambers, to have visited her privately through that passage, and to have fathered a child with her. If his testimony is accurate, he is one of the most important witnesses to the events surrounding the assassination. If his testimony is fabricated or manipulated, he may be something else entirely—a plant, a patsy, or a participant in whatever actually happened. Waluigi has learned to be careful about accepting testimony at face value, even testimony that seems emotionally authentic. Especially testimony that seems emotionally authentic. Grief can be performed. Love can be invented. And Thornpaw has had eighty-five years to construct whatever narrative serves his purposes. WAH.

Evidence

  • Claws — “The Rakasha Who Loved a Princess”
  • Hunting Spear — “The Rakasha Who Loved a Princess”
  • Extra Attack — “The Rakasha Who Loved a Princess”
  • Chief by Wisdom and Strength — “Rakasha society is organized around tribal structures led by chiefs who earn their positions through demonstrated wisdom and strength rather than hereditary succession.”
  • Eighty-Five Years of Narrative — “And Thornpaw has had eighty-five years to construct whatever narrative serves his purposes.”

description.value: Chirneros makes three attacks, one with his Pike, one with his Greatsword, and one with his Gore.

This armor consists of a seemingly endless collection of pelts spanning the decades that Chirneros has hunted the lands. Each piece is bound together by a thread of enchanted vines that shift the panels of animal skin to help camouflage him in different environments.

You have a +2 bonus to AC while wearing this armor and can change the appearance of the armor to match any animal's coloring. Once a day as a free action you gain advantage on a stealth check anywhere that animals can be found.

Melee Weapon Attack: +8 to hit, 5 ft., one target. Hit: 13 (2d8 + 4) piercing damage.

Chirneros gores his target with his vicious antlers.

Chirneros summons bestial spirits to aid him in battle and torment his foes. Chirneros may summon one of the following:

  • Two Spirit Hunters

  • One Spirit Charger

  • One Spirit Striker

Chirneros may only summon a type of spirit creature which is not yet present in the combat encounter.

The summoned beasts appear within 30 feet of Chirneros and Chirneros gains 10 temporary hit points.

The summoned beasts enter initiative order immediately, following the creature whose turn just concluded.

The creatures disappear when they reach zero hit points, or Chirneros may use a Bonus Action to dismiss them.

Chirneros manifests bestial spirits from primal Fey energy.
Chirneros is magically attuned with beasts of all kinds. He can cast several spells innately. Charisma is his spellcasting ability (Spell Save DC 15)

By means of this spell, you use an animal to deliver a message. Choose a Tiny beast you can see within range, such as a squirrel, a blue jay, or a bat. You specify a location, which you must have visited, and a recipient who matches a general description, such as "a man or woman dressed in the uniform of the town guard" or "a red-haired dwarf wearing a pointed hat." You also speak a message of up to twenty-five words. The target beast travels for the duration of the spell toward the specified location, covering about 50 miles per 24 hours for a flying messenger, or 25 miles for other animals.

When the messenger arrives, it delivers your message to the creature that you described, replicating the sound of your voice. The messenger speaks only to a creature matching the description you gave. If the messenger doesn't reach its destination before the spell ends, the message is lost, and the beast makes its way back to where you cast this spell.

At Higher Levels. If you cast this spell using a spell slot of 3rd level or higher, the duration of the spell increases by 48 hours for each slot level above 2nd.

You summon fey spirits that take the form of beasts and appear in unoccupied spaces that you can see within range. Choose one of the following options for what appears:

  • One beast of challenge rating 2 or lower
  • Two beasts of challenge rating 1 or lower
  • Four beasts of challenge rating 1/2 or lower
  • Eight beasts of challenge rating 1/4 or lower
  • Each beast is also considered fey, and it disappears when it drops to 0 hit points or when the spell ends.

The summoned creatures are friendly to you and your companions. Roll initiative for the summoned creatures as a group, which has its own turns. They obey any verbal commands that you issue to them (no action required by you). If you don't issue any commands to them, they defend themselves from hostile creatures, but otherwise take no actions.

Higher Levels. When you cast this spell using certain higher-level spell slots, you choose one of the summoning options above, and more creatures appear: twice as many with a 5th-level slot, three times as many with a 7th-level.

You gain the ability to comprehend and verbally communicate with beasts for the duration. The knowledge and awareness of many beasts is limited by their intelligence, but at minimum, beasts can give you information about nearby locations and monsters, including whatever they can perceive or have perceived within the past day. You might be able to persuade a beast to perform a small favor for you, at the DM's discretion.

Describe or name a specific kind of beast. Concentrating on the voice of nature in your surroundings, you learn the direction and distance to the closest creatureof that kind within 5 miles, if any are present.

After spending the casting time tracing magical pathways within a precious gemstone, you touch a Huge or smaller beast or plant. The target must have either no Intelligence score or an Intelligence of 3 or less. The target gains an Intelligence of 10. The target also gains the ability to speak one language you know. If the target is a plant, it gains the ability to move its limbs, roots, vines, creepers, and so forth, and it gains senses similar to a human's. Your DM chooses statistics appropriate for the awakened plant, such as the statistics for the awakened shrub or the awakened tree.

The awakened beast or plant is charmed by you for 30 days or until you or your companions do anything harmful to it. When the charmed condition ends, the awakened creature chooses whether to remain friendly to you, based on how you treated it while it was charmed.

description.value:
You summon a spirit that assumes the form of an unusually intelligent, strong, and loyal steed, creating a long-lasting bond with it. Appearing in an unoccupied space within range, the steed takes on a form that you choose, such as a warhorse, a pony, a camel, an elk, or a mastiff. (Your DM might allow other animals to be summoned as steeds.) The steed has the statistics of the chosen form, though it is a celestial, fey, or fiend (your choice) instead of its normal type. Additionally, if your steed has an Intelligence of 5 or less, its Intelligence becomes 6, and it gains the ability to understand one language of your choice that you speak.

Your steed serves you as a mount, both in combat and out, and you have an instinctive bond with it that allows you to fight as a seamless unit. While mounted on your steed, you can make any spell you cast that targets only you also target your steed.

When the steed drops to 0 hit points, it disappears, leaving behind no physical form. You can also dismiss your steed at any time as an action, causing it to disappear. In either case, casting this spell again summons the same steed, restored to its hit point maximum.

While your steed is within 1 mile of you, you can communicate with it telepathically.

You can't have more than one steed bonded by this spell at a time. As an action, you can release the steed from its bond at any time, causing it to disappear.

One Beast you can see within range must succeed on a Wisdom saving throw or have the &Reference[Charmed apply=false] condition for the duration. The target has Advantage on the save if you or your allies are fighting it. Whenever the target takes damage, it repeats the save, ending the spell on itself on a success.

You have a telepathic link with the Charmed target while the two of you are on the same plane of existence. On your turn, you can use this link to issue commands to the target (no action required), such as "Attack that creature," "Move over there," or "Fetch that object." The target does its best to obey on its turn. If it completes an order and doesn't receive further direction from you, it acts and moves as it likes, focusing on protecting itself.

You can command the target to take a Reaction but must take your own Reaction to do so.

Using a Higher-Level Spell Slot. Your Concentration can last longer with a spell slot of level 5 (up to 10 minutes), 6 (up to 1 hour), or 7+ (up to 8 hours).

Fawful's Forces packet sheet — Chortle-Bot. Built by tools/build-forge-packets.py from the NPC Forge roster data/forge/fawfuls-forces.json (entry chortle-bot): Small construct (Fawful-Bot), Unaligned; CR 1/2 (proficiency +2, to hit +4 with DEX); AC 13 (tin plating), hit points 18 (4d6+4), speed 30 ft.. A GM scene kit for the Fawful's Forces article's present (1040 BF), not a filed event; the faction article stays the authority.

The cheapest thing Fawful builds and the thing he builds most of. A Chortle-Bot is a tin bean on legs with a laugh-capacitor where a mind should be: it giggles when it walks, giggles when it stabs, and giggles loudest when a dozen of them have found something to stab together. The faction article's Fury Meter puts "Fawful-Bots" on the third rung, after the minions and the traps — these are the first Fawful-Bots, the ones the occupation turns loose in the castle's corridors by the crate.

Alone, one is a nuisance that a Palace Guard can kick over. The danger is the chorus — three or more within ten feet of each other start timing their swings to the laugh — and the burst at the end, which has cost more than one careless boot a toe. The wind-up key is the joke Fawful never fixed: he thinks nobody will get close enough to use it.

Role: swarm skirmisher · tier: Fawful-Bot · folder: Fawful's Furious Freaks / Machines of Fury.

Art

Token plate portraits/fawfuls-forces/chortle-bot.png — NPC Forge render, seed 410001, cut from a flat #FF00FF field. Prompt: Clean cel-shaded cartoon character art in the style of Mario & Luigi RPG concept art, bold dark outlines, flat colours, simple shading. A small round lime-green tin robot shaped like a bean with a huge toothy grin, two round yellow glowing eyes, a brass wind-up key in its back, short stubby brass legs and arms, holding a sparking brass prod. Full body, whole figure visible, three-quarter view, centred, isolated on a plain flat solid magenta background (#FF00FF), no floor, no ground shadow, no text, no border.

Author's Note: Please see below the entry for “Spider” which will suffice for the description of this creature.  Please note that “Giant” is a relative term and this creature is only giant in relative terms to its common size.

Spiders are one of the smallest, yet most feared, denizens of our planet.  Spiders are arachnids with eight thin legs protruding from their dual-segmented body.  Atop the spider's tiny head are eight glistening eyes with which it views the world in relative obscurity.  While the spider's eyesight may be poor regardless of the number of eyes, they have a clever trick up their sleeves: the spider's web!

Some Bug. Ingenious little architects, spiders produce a silken thread from their rears dubbed “webbing” which they use to construct elaborate homes.  Resembling something of a net, the spider's web serves a dual purpose: to capture food upon its sticky surface and to give the spider a safe place to perch away from predators.  Once an insect is trapped within the web, the spider quickly wraps the unsuspecting creature in a bundle of webbing, saving its prize for later consumption.  While all spiders are venomous in some capacity, many will not be harmful to the adventurer on their travels.  Simply avoid webs where you see them and be quite sure that the web which you see only belongs to a standard spider species, as a plethora of gigantic and magical varieties also lurk within similar webs!

Fawful's Forces packet sheet — Countess Chortlebrass. Built by tools/build-forge-packets.py from the NPC Forge roster data/forge/fawfuls-forces.json (entry countess-chortlebrass): Large humanoid (Beanish), Neutral Evil; CR 7 (proficiency +3, to hit +6 with STR); AC 16 (throne plating), hit points 127 (15d10+45), speed 30 ft., climb 20 ft.. A GM scene kit for the Fawful's Forces article's present (1040 BF), not a filed event; the faction article stays the authority.

Fawful's headmistress of helms — the Beanish noblewoman who runs the vats under Peach's Castle and decides which prisoners come out as thralls. The Countess took to the Fury Meter's logic better than anyone on the staff: she does not fight, she assigns, and the crown she wears is a rack of Hypno-Helms waiting for heads. The walking throne is her own commission; she has not touched the floor of the castle since the occupation began and regards that as a courtesy to the floor.

As a boss she is a controller first and a brawler second. The barrage puts helms on the party; the decree turns a party member for a moment; the reconstitution eats the wreckage of every construct the party has already killed. Kill the helms, keep the wrecks away from her, and knock the throne's legs out (40 hit points and under) and she is suddenly a thin woman in a chair. She does not cackle when she loses. She writes names down.

Role: controller boss · tier: lieutenant · folder: Fawful's Furious Freaks / Lieutenants of Fury.

languages.custom: Beanish; telepathy 120 ft. with helm-bound creatures

description.value: The Countess makes two Throne Claw attacks, or one Throne Claw attack and uses Fawful's Decree.
Melee Weapon Attack: reach 10 ft., one target. Hit: 2d10 + 3 slashing damage.

The Countess fixes one creature she can see within 60 feet that can hear her with the lorgnette. The target must succeed on a DC 15 Wisdom saving throw or be charmed by her until the end of her next turn; while charmed this way it immediately uses its reaction to move up to its speed and make one weapon attack against a creature of her choice. A creature that succeeds is immune to her Decree for 24 hours.

Recharge 5–6. The crown flings helms. Up to three creatures she can see within 30 feet must each succeed on a DC 15 Dexterity saving throw or take 2d6 bludgeoning damage as a Hypno-Helm lands on them: place a Hypno-Helm (this packet) attached to each creature that failed; it has latched on and the creature must make the helm's DC 13 Wisdom saving throw against Fawful's Voice at once. Helms that miss land in an empty space within 5 feet of their target and act on the Countess's initiative.

The throne rears and slams down. Each creature within 10 feet of the Countess must make a DC 15 Dexterity saving throw, taking 3d8 bludgeoning damage and falling prone on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful one.

Recharge 6. The Countess laughs and every helm in the room laughs with her. Each creature within 30 feet that can hear her must make a DC 15 Wisdom saving throw, taking 4d6 psychic damage and losing its reaction until the end of its next turn on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful one. Constructs and helm-bound creatures are unaffected.
Bonus action, 3/Day. The throne's boiler eats a destroyed Fawful construct within 30 feet (the wreck is consumed). The Countess regains 15 hit points and her Helm Barrage recharges.
Legendary action (1). The throne scuttles up to 15 feet without provoking opportunity attacks.
Legendary action (1). The Countess makes one Throne Claw attack.
Legendary action (2). The Countess uses Fawful's Decree.

The Countess's crown is built of Hypno-Helms and her mind is her own; she can't be charmed, and any creature charmed by a Hypno-Helm within 120 feet of her is charmed by her too and obeys her telepathic orders over the helm's.

The Countess rides a walking mechanical throne; the statblock is the pair. She can't be knocked prone while the throne stands, and the throne lets her climb. When she is reduced to 40 hit points or fewer the throne's legs buckle: her speed drops to 10 feet and she loses Throne Stomp and the Scuttle legendary action.
If the Countess fails a saving throw, she can choose to succeed instead.

description.value:
You create a magical effect within range. Choose the effect from the options below. If you cast this spell multiple times, you can have up to three of its non-instantaneous effects active at a time.

Sensory Effect. You create an instantaneous, harmless sensory effect, such as a shower of sparks, a puff of wind, faint musical notes, or an odd odor.

Fire Play. You instantaneously light or snuff out a candle, a torch, or a small campfire.

Clean or Soil. You instantaneously clean or soil an object no larger than 1 cubic foot.

Minor Sensation. You chill, warm, or flavor up to 1 cubic foot of nonliving material for 1 hour.

Magic Mark. You make a color, a small mark, or a symbol appear on an object or a surface for 1 hour.

Minor Creation. You create a nonmagical trinket or an illusory image that can fit in your hand. It lasts until the end of your next turn. A trinket can deal no damage and has no monetary worth.

This spell repairs a single break or tear in an object you touch, such as a broken chain link, two halves of a broken key, a torn cloak, or a leaking wineskin. As long as the break or tear is no larger than 1 foot in any dimension, you mend it, leaving no trace of the former damage.

This spell can physically repair a magic item, but it can't restore magic to such an object.

You touch one Large or smaller object that isn't being worn or carried by someone else. Until the spell ends, the object sheds Bright Light in a 20-foot radius and Dim Light for an additional 20 feet. The light can be colored as you like.

Covering the object with something opaque blocks the light. The spell ends if you cast it again.

For the duration, you sense the presence of magical effects within 30 feet of yourself. If you sense such effects, you can take the Magic action to see a faint aura around any visible creature or object in the area that bears the magic, and if an effect was created by a spell, you learn the spell's school of magic.

The spell is blocked by 1 foot of stone, dirt, or wood; 1 inch of metal; or a thin sheet of lead.

You touch an object throughout the spell's casting. If the object is a magic item or some other magical object, you learn its properties and how to use them, whether it requires Attunement, and how many charges it has, if any. You learn whether any ongoing spells are affecting the item and what they are. If the item was created by a spell, you learn that spell's name.

If you instead touch a creature throughout the casting, you learn which ongoing spells, if any, are currently affecting it.

Three illusory duplicates of yourself appear in your space. Until the spell ends, the duplicates move with you and mimic your actions, shifting position so it's impossible to track which image is real.

Each time a creature hits you with an attack roll during the spell's duration, roll a [[/r (@flags.dnd-players-handbook.mirrorImages)d6kh1cs>2#Duplicate destroyed]]{d6 for each} of your remaining duplicates. If any of the d6s rolls a 3 or higher, one of the duplicates is hit instead of you, and the duplicate is destroyed. The duplicates otherwise ignore all other damage and effects. The spell ends when all three duplicates are destroyed.

A creature is unaffected by this spell if it has the &Reference[blinded apply=false] condition, &Reference[blindsight], or &Reference[truesight].

Your body becomes blurred. For the duration, any creature has Disadvantage on attack rolls against you. An attacker is immune to this effect if it perceives you with &Reference[blindsight] or &Reference[truesight].

effects.name: Blurred
effects.description: For the duration, any creature has Disadvantage on attack rolls against you. An attacker is immune to this effect if it perceives you with Blindsight or Truesight.

description.value: You touch a closed door, window, gate, container, or hatch and magically lock it for the duration. This lock can't be unlocked by any nonmagical means. You and any creatures you designate when you cast the spell can open and close the object despite the lock. You can also set a password that, when spoken within 5 feet of the object, unlocks it for 1 minute.

Using a Higher-Level Spell Slot. You can target one additional Humanoid for each spell slot level above 2.

description.value: You attempt to interrupt a creature in the process of casting a spell. The creature makes a Constitution saving throw. On a failed save, the spell dissipates with no effect, and the action, Bonus Action, or Reaction used to cast it is wasted. If that spell was cast with a spell slot, the slot isn't expended.

Using a Higher-Level Spell Slot. The damage increases by 1d6 for each spell slot level above 3.
