description.value: Green T's build is a martial/social hybrid the campaign has no published class for. Hit Die d10. Runs on three pillars: the giant form, the concealed firearm, and a calm that reads as harmlessness. Proficiency bonus +3.
Outwardly an ordinary Toad, which is the point. Carries a latent capacity for enormous physical growth that nobody suspected across an entire criminal career.

You ran an organisation where threats were delivered politely and the tea was genuinely excellent. Proficiencies: Deception and Insight; surviving Tea Leaf Syndicate contacts; you know how a room is seated and why.

Bonus Action; 2/Long Rest; up to 10 minutes. Your size becomes Huge or larger. Gain +4 Strength for the duration, your reach increases by 10 feet, your melee attacks deal an extra 1d8 bludgeoning, and you can attempt to shake terrain within 30 feet (DC 14 Dexterity save or prone). You count as difficult terrain for enemies who try to pass you.

The cost curve. Each round after the third, take 1d6 unavoidable exhaustion-track damage and make a DC 12 Constitution save; on a failure the form ends. Being Huge is also being a larger target — attacks against you from Small or smaller swarms have advantage. Established at the Syndicate Showdown and paid for publicly in the Scorncrow grove.

While in Giant Form you may lift a willing ally to your shoulder as part of your movement. They gain a 30-foot vantage, advantage on Perception checks to spot at range, and cover from ground-level attacks. Used at the grove to lift Remi to spot the Scorncrow.

When an enemy has dismissed, demoted, or underestimated you in a social scene, your first attack against them in the following combat has advantage and scores a critical on 19–20. You may also make one Perception or Investigation check to map a room while apparently doing nothing. Orangus Cornelius seated him with the children and did not survive the decision.
Advantage on saves against being frightened or goaded, and on Deception checks to appear harmless, unarmed, or uninterested. He has never once raised his voice to make a threat land.
Once per turn, if you have not moved this turn, add +1d6 to a ranged attack's damage against a target you can see clearly. He remembers a fight as sightlines and timing, not as a sequence of blows.

Reaction, 1/short rest. When an ally within 30 feet is reduced to 0 hit points, you may move up to your speed toward them without provoking opportunity attacks and make one attack against the creature responsible. Everything gets settled; nothing is left ragged.

A concealable firearm Green T has repeatedly smuggled into rooms where weapons were categorically not permitted. How remains unexplained and he declines to explain it.

Ranged Weapon Attack: Dexterity, range 40/120, 1d10 piercing, loading, reload 1. Loaded with silver by default.

Ammunition for the revolver. Silver overcomes the resistances of vampires, lycanthropes, and several things at the Shadow Estate that assumed they were safe. One of these ended Orangus Cornelius's evening.

Held in custody, not owned. One of the four portal artifacts, broken in a ghost's bedroom and mended by Remi Akamatsu casting Mending. Green T requested the components, Markop supplied the base, Remi supplied the fragment.

Wario attempted immediate theft and was stopped by Markop. Under the resulting bargain Wario helps with Scarecrow and expects the mirror afterward. GM note: this is an open obligation, not settled property — it should cost him something.
Tasteful, well cut, quietly reinforced, and possessed of more pockets than its silhouette can account for. AC 12 + Dexterity modifier.

Genuinely excellent tea and the equipment to serve it properly. Used to open negotiations, stall for time, and establish that the person pouring is not in a hurry. During a short rest, one ally who drinks gains advantage on their next Charisma check.

An Inspiring Performer of Music, Dance, and Magic
Evyn Fong

Invoking magic through music, dance, and verse, Bards are expert at inspiring others, soothing hurts, disheartening foes, and creating illusions. Bards believe the multiverse was spoken into existence and that remnants of its Words of Creation still resound and glimmer on every plane of existence. Bardic magic attempts to harness those words, which transcend any language.

Anything can inspire a new song or tale, so Bards are fascinated by almost everything. They become masters of many things, including performing music, working magic, and making jests.

A Bard's life is spent traveling, gathering lore, telling stories, and living on the gratitude of audiences, much like any other entertainer. But Bards' depth of knowledge and mastery of magic sets them apart.

Level 1: Bardic Inspiration

You can supernaturally inspire others through words, music, or dance. This inspiration is represented by your Bardic Inspiration die, which is a [[/r d6]].

Using Bardic Inspiration. As a @variantrule[Bonus Action|XPHB], you can inspire another creature within 60 feet of yourself who can see or hear you. That creature gains one of your Bardic Inspiration dice. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time.

Once within the next hour when the creature fails a @variantrule[D20 Test|XPHB], the creature can roll the Bardic Inspiration die and add the number rolled to the [[/r d20]], potentially turning the failure into a success. A Bardic Inspiration die is expended when it's rolled.

Number of Uses. You can confer a Bardic Inspiration die a number of times equal to your Charisma modifier (minimum of once), and you regain all expended uses when you finish a @variantrule[Long Rest|XPHB].

At Higher Levels. Your Bardic Inspiration die changes when you reach certain Bard levels, as shown in the Bardic Die column of the Bard Features table. The die becomes a [[/r d8]] at level 5, a [[/r d10]] at level 10, and a [[/r d12]] at level 15.

Level 1: Spellcasting

You have learned to cast spells through your bardic arts. See chapter 7 for the rules on spellcasting. The information below details how you use those rules with Bard spells, which appear in the Bard spell list later in the class's description.

Cantrips. You know two cantrips of your choice from the Bard spell list. @spell[Dancing Lights|XPHB] and @spell[Vicious Mockery|XPHB] are recommended.

Whenever you gain a Bard level, you can replace one of your cantrips with another cantrip of your choice from the Bard spell list.

When you reach Bard levels 4 and 10, you learn another cantrip of your choice from the Bard spell list, as shown in the Cantrips column of the Bard Features table.

Spell Slots. The Bard Features table shows how many spell slots you have to cast your level 1+ spells. You regain all expended slots when you finish a @variantrule[Long Rest|XPHB].

Prepared Spells of Level 1+. You prepare the list of level 1+ spells that are available for you to cast with this feature. To start, choose four level 1 spells from the Bard spell list. @spell[Charm Person|XPHB], @spell[Color Spray|XPHB], @spell[Dissonant Whispers|XPHB], and @spell[Healing Word|XPHB] are recommended.

The number of spells on your list increases as you gain Bard levels, as shown in the Prepared Spells column of the Bard Features table. Whenever that number increases, choose additional spells from the Bard spell list until the number of spells on your list matches the number on the table. The chosen spells must be of a level for which you have spell slots. For example, if you're a level 3 Bard, your list of prepared spells can include six spells of levels 1 and 2 in any combination.

If another Bard feature gives you spells that you always have prepared, those spells don't count against the number of spells you can prepare with this feature, but those spells otherwise count as Bard spells for you.

Changing Your Prepared Spells. Whenever you gain a Bard level, you can replace one spell on your list with another Bard spell for which you have spell slots.

Spellcasting Ability. Charisma is your spellcasting ability for your Bard spells.

Spellcasting Focus. You can use a @item[Musical Instrument|XPHB] as a @variantrule[Spellcasting Focus|XPHB] for your Bard spells.

Level 2: Expertise

You gain @variantrule[Expertise|XPHB] in two of your skill proficiencies of your choice. &Reference[skill=Performance] and &Reference[skill=Persuasion] are recommended if you have proficiency in them.

At Bard level 9, you gain @variantrule[Expertise|XPHB] in two more of your skill proficiencies of your choice.

Level 2: Jack of All Trades

You can add half your @variantrule[Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus] (round down) to any ability check you make that uses a skill proficiency you lack and that doesn't otherwise use your @variantrule[Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus].

For example, if you make a Strength (&Reference[skill=Athletics]) check and lack &Reference[skill=Athletics] proficiency, you can add half your @variantrule[Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus] to the check.

A Bard's Repertoire

Does your Bard beat a @item[drum|XPHB] while chanting the deeds of ancient heroes? Strum a @item[lute|XPHB] while crooning romantic tunes? Perform arias of stirring power? Recite dramatic monologues from classic tragedies? Use the rhythm of a folk dance to coordinate the movement of allies in battle? Compose naughty limericks?

When you play a Bard, consider the style of artistic performance you favor, the moods you might invoke, and the themes that inspire your own creations. Are your poems inspired by moments of natural beauty, or are they brooding reflections on loss? Do you prefer lofty hymns or rowdy tavern songs? Are you drawn to laments for the fallen or celebrations of joy? Do you dance merry jigs or perform elaborate interpretive choreography? Do you focus on one style of performance or strive to master them all?

Level 3: Bard Subclass

You gain a Bard subclass of your choice. A subclass is a specialization that grants you features at certain Bard levels. For the rest of your career, you gain each of your subclass's features that are of your Bard level or lower.

Level 4: Ability Score Improvement

You gain the @feat[Ability Score Improvement|XPHB] feat or another feat of your choice for which you qualify. You gain this feature again at Bard levels 8, 12, and 16.

Level 5: Font of Inspiration

You now regain all your expended uses of Bardic Inspiration when you finish a @variantrule[Short Rest|XPHB|Short] or @variantrule[Long Rest|XPHB].

In addition, you can expend a spell slot (no action required) to regain one expended use of Bardic Inspiration.

Level 6: Subclass Feature

You gain a feature from your Bard Subclass.

Level 7: Countercharm

You can use musical notes or words of power to disrupt mind-influencing effects. If you or a creature within 30 feet of you fails a saving throw against an effect that applies the &Reference[condition=Charmed] or &Reference[condition=Frightened] condition, you can take a @variantrule[Reaction|XPHB] to cause the save to be rerolled, and the new roll has @variantrule[Advantage|XPHB].

Level 8: Ability Score Improvement

You gain the @feat[Ability Score Improvement|XPHB] feat or another feat of your choice for which you qualify.

Level 9: Expertise

You gain @variantrule[Expertise|XPHB] in two of your Skill Proficiencies of your choice.

Level 10: Magical Secrets

You've learned secrets from various magical traditions. Whenever you reach a Bard level (including this level) and the Prepared Spells number in the Bard Features table increases, you can choose any of your new prepared spells from the Bard, Cleric, Druid, and Wizard spell lists, and the chosen spells count as Bard spells for you (see a class's section for its spell list). In addition, whenever you replace a spell prepared for this class, you can replace it with a spell from those lists.

Level 12: Ability Score Improvement

You gain the @feat[Ability Score Improvement|XPHB] feat or another feat of your choice for which you qualify.

Level 14: Subclass Feature

You gain a feature from your Bard Subclass.

Level 16: Ability Score Improvement

You gain the @feat[Ability Score Improvement|XPHB] feat or another feat of your choice for which you qualify.

Level 18: Superior Inspiration

When you roll @variantrule[Initiative|XPHB], you regain expended uses of Bardic Inspiration until you have two if you have fewer than that.

Level 19: Epic Boon

You gain an Epic Boon feat or another feat of your choice for which you qualify. @feat[Boon of Spell Recall|XPHB] is recommended.

Level 20: Words of Creation

You have mastered two of the Words of Creation: the words of life and death. You therefore always have the @spell[Power Word Heal|XPHB] and @spell[Power Word Kill|XPHB] spells prepared. When you cast either spell, you can target a second creature with it if that creature is within 10 feet of the first target.

Mattia Rangoni

College of Adventurers

Be a Master of Classes

Bards from the College of Adventurers learn from heroes of old and stories of legend. Bards are jacks of all trades, and, for the College of Adventurers, this statement rings even truer. They combine all the skills of their companions into one, allowing them to be versatile and supportive. While not having a direct goal, many adventurer-studying Bards live to tell tales of other heroes or seek to create their own. Stories of great deeds, of desperate cunning, of magical anomalies, or of godly might fuel these Bards.

Level 3: Talented Adventurer

You learn an adventurer's talent of your choice from the "Adventurer's Talent Options" section later in this subclass's description. You learn an additional adventurer's talent of your choice when you reach Bard levels 6 and 14.

Barbarian. You've learned to fight with primal ferocity.

As a @variantrule[Bonus Action|XPHB] while you aren't wearing Heavy armor, you can enter a rampage for 1 minute. During this time, you have @variantrule[Resistance|XPHB] to Bludgeoning, Piercing, and Slashing damage, and you can't maintain @status[Concentration|XPHB]. Your rampage ends early if you use a @variantrule[Bonus Action|XPHB] or have the &Reference[condition=Incapacitated] condition.

Once you use this talent, you can't use it again until you finish a @variantrule[Long Rest|XPHB].

Cleric. You've gained the ability to channel divine energy directly from the gods, emboldening allies and sanctifying their attacks. As a @variantrule[Bonus Action|XPHB], choose a creature within 30 feet of you. For 10 minutes, the target gains @variantrule[Temporary Hit Points|XPHB] equal to half your Bard level plus your Charisma modifier. While a creature has @variantrule[Temporary Hit Points|XPHB] granted by this talent, it can choose to lose all remaining @variantrule[Temporary Hit Points|XPHB] when it hits a creature with an attack made with a weapon or @variantrule[Unarmed Strike|XPHB], dealing extra Radiant damage equal to the number of @variantrule[Temporary Hit Points|XPHB] lost.

Once you use this talent, you can't use it again until you finish a @variantrule[Short Rest|XPHB|Short] or @variantrule[Long Rest|XPHB].

Druid. You can cast the @spell[Polymorph|XPHB] spell without expending a spell slot. When you cast the @spell[Polymorph|XPHB] spell with this talent, you can target yourself only and the maximum @variantrule[Challenge Rating|XPHB] of the Beast you can transform into equals half your Druid level.

Once you cast the spell using this talent, you can't do so again until you finish a @variantrule[Long Rest|XPHB].

Fighter. You gain proficiency with martial weapons and training with @item[Shield|XPHB|Shields]. In addition, you gain a Fighting Style feat of your choice.

Monk. While you aren't wearing armor or wielding a @item[Shield|XPHB], your base @variantrule[Armor Class|XPHB] equals 10 plus your Dexterity and Charisma modifiers. You can use your Dexterity modifier instead of your Strength modifier for the attack and damage rolls of your @variantrule[Unarmed Strike|XPHB|Unarmed Strikes], and you can roll [[/r 1d6]] in place of the normal damage of your @variantrule[Unarmed Strike|XPHB]. In addition, after you cast a spell that has a casting time of an action or take the @action[Attack|XPHB] action, you can make one attack with an @variantrule[Unarmed Strike|XPHB] as a @variantrule[Bonus Action|XPHB].

Paladin. Once per turn, when you hit a creature with a melee attack using a weapon or @variantrule[Unarmed Strike|XPHB], you can expend a spell slot to deal an extra [[/r 1d6]] Radiant damage to the target, plus another [[/r 1d6]] per level of the spell slot.

The damage increases by [[/r 1d6]] if the target is a Fiend or an Undead.

Once you use this talent, you must finish a @variantrule[Short Rest|XPHB] or @variantrule[Long Rest|XPHB] before you can use it again.

Ranger. You always have the @spell[Hunter's Mark|XPHB] spell prepared. You can cast this spell using a 5th-level spell slot without expending a spell slot.

Once you cast the spell using this talent, you can't do so again until you finish a @variantrule[Long Rest|XPHB].

Rogue. You've adopted the quick thinking of heroes who have outsmarted their foes. On your turn, you can take one of the following actions as a @variantrule[Bonus Action|XPHB]: @action[Dash|XPHB], @action[Disengage|XPHB], or @action[Hide|XPHB].

Sorcerer. Choose one of the following Metamagic Options available to the Sorcerer class: @optfeature[Careful Spell|XPHB], @optfeature[Distant Spell|XPHB], @optfeature[Empowered Spell|XPHB], @optfeature[Extended Spell|XPHB], @optfeature[Seeking Spell|XPHB], @optfeature[Subtle Spell|XPHB], or @optfeature[Transmuted Spell|XPHB].

When you cast a Bard spell, you can apply that Metamagic Option as if you had paid its Sorcery Point cost.

Once you use this talent, you can't use it again until you finish a @variantrule[Short Rest|XPHB] or @variantrule[Long Rest|XPHB].

Warlock. You learn one Eldritch Invocation of your choice. If an invocation has a level requirement, use your Bard level.

When you gain a level in this class, you can choose one of the invocations you know and replace it with another invocation for which you qualify.

Wizard. You prepare any two spells from the Wizard spell list that are of a level you can cast. These count as Bard spells for you but do not count against your number of Prepared Spells.

When you gain a level in this class, you can choose one of the Wizard spells you have prepared and replace it with another spell from the Wizard spell list of a level you can cast.

Level 3: Party Planner

While a creature has a Bardic Inspiration die from you, it can use a @variantrule[Bonus Action|XPHB] to take the @action[Help|XPHB] action.

Level 6: Well-Rounded

You gain proficiency with one type of @item[Artisan's Tools|XPHB] of your choice, you gain proficiency in one skill of your choice, and you know one language of your choice.

Level 14: Improvisational Talent

When you finish a @variantrule[Long Rest|XPHB], you can choose one adventurer's talent you know and replace it with one you don't.

You can supernaturally inspire others through words, music, or dance. This inspiration is represented by your Bardic Inspiration die, which is a [[/r d6]].

Using Bardic Inspiration. As a @variantrule[Bonus Action|XPHB], you can inspire another creature within 60 feet of yourself who can see or hear you. That creature gains one of your Bardic Inspiration dice. A creature can have only one Bardic Inspiration die at a time.

Once within the next hour when the creature fails a @variantrule[D20 Test|XPHB], the creature can roll the Bardic Inspiration die and add the number rolled to the [[/r d20]], potentially turning the failure into a success. A Bardic Inspiration die is expended when it's rolled.

Number of Uses. You can confer a Bardic Inspiration die a number of times equal to your Charisma modifier (minimum of once), and you regain all expended uses when you finish a @variantrule[Long Rest|XPHB].

At Higher Levels. Your Bardic Inspiration die changes when you reach certain Bard levels, as shown in the Bardic Die column of the Bard Features table. The die becomes a [[/r d8]] at level 5, a [[/r d10]] at level 10, and a [[/r d12]] at level 15.

description.value:
You have learned to cast spells through your bardic arts. See chapter 7 for the rules on spellcasting. The information below details how you use those rules with Bard spells, which appear in the Bard spell list later in the class's description.

Cantrips. You know two cantrips of your choice from the Bard spell list. @spell[Dancing Lights|XPHB] and @spell[Vicious Mockery|XPHB] are recommended.

Whenever you gain a Bard level, you can replace one of your cantrips with another cantrip of your choice from the Bard spell list.

When you reach Bard levels 4 and 10, you learn another cantrip of your choice from the Bard spell list, as shown in the Cantrips column of the Bard Features table.

Spell Slots. The Bard Features table shows how many spell slots you have to cast your level 1+ spells. You regain all expended slots when you finish a @variantrule[Long Rest|XPHB].

Prepared Spells of Level 1+. You prepare the list of level 1+ spells that are available for you to cast with this feature. To start, choose four level 1 spells from the Bard spell list. @spell[Charm Person|XPHB], @spell[Color Spray|XPHB], @spell[Dissonant Whispers|XPHB], and @spell[Healing Word|XPHB] are recommended.

The number of spells on your list increases as you gain Bard levels, as shown in the Prepared Spells column of the Bard Features table. Whenever that number increases, choose additional spells from the Bard spell list until the number of spells on your list matches the number on the table. The chosen spells must be of a level for which you have spell slots. For example, if you're a level 3 Bard, your list of prepared spells can include six spells of levels 1 and 2 in any combination.

If another Bard feature gives you spells that you always have prepared, those spells don't count against the number of spells you can prepare with this feature, but those spells otherwise count as Bard spells for you.

Changing Your Prepared Spells. Whenever you gain a Bard level, you can replace one spell on your list with another Bard spell for which you have spell slots.

Spellcasting Ability. Charisma is your spellcasting ability for your Bard spells.

Spellcasting Focus. You can use a @item[Musical Instrument|XPHB] as a @variantrule[Spellcasting Focus|XPHB] for your Bard spells.

You gain @variantrule[Expertise|XPHB] in two of your skill proficiencies of your choice. &Reference[skill=Performance] and &Reference[skill=Persuasion] are recommended if you have proficiency in them.

At Bard level 9, you gain @variantrule[Expertise|XPHB] in two more of your skill proficiencies of your choice.

You can add half your @variantrule[Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus] (round down) to any ability check you make that uses a skill proficiency you lack and that doesn't otherwise use your @variantrule[Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus].

For example, if you make a Strength (&Reference[skill=Athletics]) check and lack &Reference[skill=Athletics] proficiency, you can add half your @variantrule[Proficiency|XPHB|Proficiency Bonus] to the check.

A Bard's Repertoire

Does your Bard beat a @item[drum|XPHB] while chanting the deeds of ancient heroes? Strum a @item[lute|XPHB] while crooning romantic tunes? Perform arias of stirring power? Recite dramatic monologues from classic tragedies? Use the rhythm of a folk dance to coordinate the movement of allies in battle? Compose naughty limericks?

When you play a Bard, consider the style of artistic performance you favor, the moods you might invoke, and the themes that inspire your own creations. Are your poems inspired by moments of natural beauty, or are they brooding reflections on loss? Do you prefer lofty hymns or rowdy tavern songs? Are you drawn to laments for the fallen or celebrations of joy? Do you dance merry jigs or perform elaborate interpretive choreography? Do you focus on one style of performance or strive to master them all?

biography.value:
Hammer Bro — The Elite Who Earned It

Hammer Bros are the Koopa Troop's elite infantry—koopas who distinguished themselves through combat performance and were promoted to a specialized role that combines armored durability with ranged firepower through the ancient koopa art of throwing hammers at things until those things stop being problems. They wear helmets that standard Troopas don't receive, carry an apparently infinite supply of hammers that they produce from somewhere nobody has ever adequately explained, and operate in paired teams that coordinate their throws to create overlapping fields of hammers that make approaching them an exercise in pain avoidance.

The hammers are the mystery. Hammer Bros throw hammers continuously during combat—not one or two, but DOZENS, an unending stream of spinning metal that arcs over intervening obstacles and descends on targets with trajectories that defy simple ballistics. Where the hammers come from is the subject of intense speculation among Mushroom Kingdom intelligence analysts. Some theories suggest hammerspace—a pocket dimension from which the hammers are summoned. Others suggest rapid materialization through innate magic that Hammer Bros themselves don't understand. The most prosaic theory involves hidden compartments in the shell, which would explain the hammers but not the apparent unlimited supply.

Hammer Bros are proud. They earned their helmets through performance, and they maintain their status through continued excellence. A Hammer Bro who misses consistently is demoted to standard Troopa duty, which is considered humiliating enough to motivate accuracy that borders on supernatural. They work in pairs because paired Hammer Bros are exponentially more dangerous than individual ones—while one throws, the other repositions, creating a rotating barrage that never stops and never comes from the same angle twice.
biography.public: A helmeted koopa with an expression of professional determination and a hammer in each hand, with more hammers visible somewhere behind him in quantities that shouldn't be possible.

description.value:
The Hammer Bro's signature attack: a rapid-fire barrage of thrown hammers that arc over obstacles and descend on targets with trajectories calculated through instinct rather than conscious math. Each hammer is a standard construction hammer—metal head, wooden handle, nothing magical about it individually—but the VOLUME and ACCURACY of the throws transforms mundane tools into a devastating ranged attack.

As an action, a Hammer Bro throws two hammers at targets it can see within 40 feet. Each hammer requires a separate attack roll (+5 to hit) and deals 1d8 + 3 bludgeoning damage on a hit. The hammers arc over half cover and three-quarters cover (though not total cover), reflecting the Hammer Bro's trained ability to throw in parabolic trajectories that bypass obstacles between thrower and target.

The unlimited supply remains unexplained. After combat, hammers thrown by Hammer Bros are found at impact sites as normal, non-magical hammers. They don't disappear. They don't return. New ones simply appear in the Hammer Bro's hands when needed. Investigation into this phenomenon has been classified as "not worth the headache" by the Mages' Guild.
description.chat: Hammers arc through the air in quantities that shouldn't be possible, descending on targets with the inevitability of rain and considerably more impact.

unidentified.name: Infinite Hammer Throws
unidentified.description: This creature throws hammers in rapid succession from an apparently unlimited supply, arcing them over obstacles to reach targets.

description.value:
A reinforced helmet that distinguishes Hammer Bros from standard Troopas and provides protection against the overhead attacks that are the primary threat to koopa infantry. The helmet is earned through performance and maintained through continued excellence—losing or damaging a helmet without adequate justification results in demotion that carries social stigma among koopa military culture.

The helmet provides +1 AC (already calculated in the Hammer Bro's statistics) and grants immunity to the critical hit bonus damage from attacks originating above—the specific vulnerability that defines standard koopa infantry is partially mitigated for the elite who earned the right to wear head protection.
description.chat: The helmet says 'I earned this.' The dent in the helmet says 'and this is why I needed it.'

unidentified.name: Elite Infantry Helmet
unidentified.description: A reinforced helmet that marks its wearer as elite infantry, providing protection that standard soldiers don't receive.

description.value:
Hammer Bros operate in paired teams that coordinate their attacks for maximum effectiveness. When two Hammer Bros are within 15 feet of each other and attacking the same target, both gain advantage on their hammer throw attack rolls as the dual barrage from different angles makes effective dodging nearly impossible. Additionally, when one Hammer Bro of a pair is attacked, the other can use its reaction to throw a hammer at the attacker (+5 to hit, 1d8 + 3 bludgeoning damage), discouraging enemies from engaging either member of the pair individually.

Breaking a Hammer Bro pair—killing one, separating them, or forcing one to retreat—immediately reduces the survivor's effectiveness and morale. A lone Hammer Bro has disadvantage on attack rolls for 1 round after its partner is eliminated, as the coordination reflexes trained into paired operation produce hesitation when the expected partner isn't there.
description.chat: They work in pairs because paired hammers create patterns that single hammers can't. Breaking the pair is priority one. Surviving the pair is priority zero.

description.value:
Hammer Bros hop. It's part of their fighting style—a rhythmic bouncing that keeps them in motion, makes them harder to hit, and provides the elevated launch angle that allows their hammer arcs to clear obstacles. The hopping looks ridiculous from a distance and is extremely effective from combat range, as the constant vertical movement complicates targeting for enemies trying to return fire.

While hopping (which Hammer Bros do automatically during combat), attacks against them have disadvantage if the attacker is at the same elevation or lower. Attacks from above are unaffected—the hopping provides lateral evasion, not overhead protection. The hopping also allows Hammer Bros to move across gaps up to 10 feet wide without requiring ability checks, their rhythmic bouncing carrying them across spaces that would require standard Troopas to find alternate routes.
description.chat: Hop. Throw. Hop. Throw. The rhythm is annoying and effective in exactly equal measure.

The Hammer Bro who held the west passage until the ceiling shook, threw a hammer at the dragon's eye, missed, hit a traitor, and did not stop to find out whether the result was politically complicated. When Bowser shouted for him to hold, he shouted back that he had held. Then he retreated, and took the surviving Goombas with him.

The record's verdict stands on the sheet: the retreat was the first honest order anybody followed all night. The west passage was no longer a position. It was a place where the ceiling was about to become a floor.

description.value: The mermaid can breathe air and water.

The mermaid covers herself and anything she is wearing or carrying with a magical illusion that makes her look like a beautiful creature of her general size and humanoid shape, albeit with the lower half of her form being that of a fish. The effect ends if the mermaid takes a bonus action to end it or if she dies.

The changes wrought by this effect fail to hold up to physical inspection. For example, the mermaid could appear to have no claws, but someone touching her hand might feel the claws. Otherwise, a creature must take an action to visually inspect the illusion and succeed on a DC 16 Intelligence (Investigation) check to discern that the mermaid is disguised.

Melee Weapon Attack:+5 to hit, 5 ft., one target. Hit: 10 (2d6 + 3) slashing damage.

 

The Mermaid attacks with her Claws.

Any humanoid that starts its turn within 120 feet of the mermaid and can hear her singing must make a DC 13 Wisdom saving throw. On a failed save, the creature is charmed for 1 minute. A creature can repeat the saving throw at the end of each of its turns, with disadvantage if the mermaid is within line of sight, ending the effect on itself on a success.

If a creature's saving throw is successful or the effect ends for it, the creature is immune to the mermaid's Beguiling Song for the next 24 hours.

Creatures that are deaf are immune to this ability and automatically succeed on their saving throw.

The Mermaid begins to sing a bewitching song that winds its way into the minds of those who listed. Any humanoid that starts its turn within 120 feet of the mermaid while she is singing and can hear her must make a Wisdom saving throw.

The mermaid targets one charmed creature she can see within 60 ft. of her. If the target can see the mermaid, it must succeed on a DC 13 Wisdom saving throw against this magic or gain 2 levels of exhaustion.

The mermaid targets one charmed creature she can see within 60 ft. of her. If the target can see the mermaid, it must make a Wisdom saving throw against this magic.

This necklace has [[/r 1d6 + 3]] pearls making up its length. You can use an action to detach a bead and throw it up to 60 feet away. When it reaches the end of its trajectory, the bead detonates in a huge blast of freezing cold sea water.

Use a 3rd-level Fireball spell (save DC 15) with the following modifications: The spell instead deals cold damage and creates a massive blast of ice cold sea water conjured from the depths of the darkest, deepest, coldest ocean in the faerie plane. This water ball drenches everything in the radius, extinguishing open flames, and knocking around unattended objects.

You can hurl multiple beads, or even the whole necklace, as one action. When you do so, increase the level of the water blast by 1 for each bead beyond the first.

**Foundry note: the 9 charges represent the maximum number of beads possible to find; please adjust as required. The Other Formula button can be used to roll the additional damage for extra beads thrown.

You are a member of an artisan's guild, skilled in a particular field and closely associated with other artisans. You are a well-established part of the mercantile world, freed by talent and wealth from the constraints of a feudal social order. You learned your skills as an apprentice to a master artisan, under the sponsorship of your guild, until you became a master in your own right.

  • Skill Proficiencies: @skill[Insight], @skill[Persuasion]

  • Tool Proficiencies: One type of artisan's tools

  • Languages: One of your choice

  • Equipment: A set of artisan's tools (one of your choice), a letter of introduction from your guild, a set of @item[traveler's clothes|phb], and a belt @item[pouch|phb] containing 15 gp

Feature: Guild Membership[–]

As an established and respected member of a guild, you can rely on certain benefits that membership provides. Your fellow guild members will provide you with lodging and food if necessary, and pay for your funeral if needed. In some cities and towns, a guildhall offers a central place to meet other members of your profession, which can be a good place to meet potential patrons, allies, or hirelings.

Guilds often wield tremendous political power. If you are accused of a crime, your guild will support you if a good case can be made for your innocence or the crime is justifiable. You can also gain access to powerful political figures through the guild, if you are a member in good standing. Such connections might require the donation of money or magic items to the guild's coffers.

You must pay dues of 5 gp per month to the guild. If you miss payments, you must make up back dues to remain in the guild's good graces.

Specialty[–]

Guilds are generally found in cities large enough to support several artisans practicing the same trade. However, your guild might instead be a loose network of artisans who each work in a different village within a larger realm. Work with your DM to determine the nature of your guild. You can select your guild business from the Guild Business table or roll randomly.

[[/r d20]]Guild Business
1Alchemists and apothecaries
2Armorers, locksmiths, and finesmiths
3Brewers, distillers, and vintners
4Calligraphers, scribes, and scriveners
5Carpenters, roofers, and plasterers
6Cartographers, surveyors, and chart-makers
7Cobblers and shoemakers
8Cooks and bakers
9Glassblowers and glaziers
10Jewelers and gemcutters
11Leatherworkers, skinners, and tanners
12Masons and stonecutters
13Painters, limners, and sign-makers
14Potters and tile-makers
15Shipwrights and sail-makers
16Smiths and metal-forgers
17Tinkers, pewterers, and casters
18Wagon-makers and wheelwrights
19Weavers and dyers
20Woodcarvers, coopers, and bowyers

Suggested Characteristics[–]

Guild artisans are among the most ordinary people in the world—until they set down their tools and take up an adventuring career. They understand the value of hard work and the importance of community, but they're vulnerable to sins of greed and covetousness.

[[/r d8]]Personality Trait
1I believe that anything worth doing is worth doing right. I can't help it—I'm a perfectionist.
2I'm a snob who looks down on those who can't appreciate fine art.
3I always want to know how things work and what makes people tick.
4I'm full of witty aphorisms and have a proverb for every occasion.
5I'm rude to people who lack my commitment to hard work and fair play.
6I like to talk at length about my profession.
7I don't part with my money easily and will haggle tirelessly to get the best deal possible.
8I'm well known for my work, and I want to make sure everyone appreciates it. I'm always taken aback when people haven't heard of me.
[[/r d6]]Ideal
1Community. It is the duty of all civilized people to strengthen the bonds of community and the security of civilization. (Lawful)
2Generosity. My talents were given to me so that I could use them to benefit the world. (Good)
3Freedom. Everyone should be free to pursue his or her own livelihood. (Chaotic)
4Greed. I'm only in it for the money. (Evil)
5People. I'm committed to the people I care about, not to ideals. (Neutral)
6Aspiration. I work hard to be the best there is at my craft. (Any)
[[/r d6]]Bond
1The workshop where I learned my trade is the most important place in the world to me.
2I created a great work for someone, and then found them unworthy to receive it. I'm still looking for someone worthy.
3I owe my guild a great debt for forging me into the person I am today.
4I pursue wealth to secure someone's love.
5One day I will return to my guild and prove that I am the greatest artisan of them all.
6I will get revenge on the evil forces that destroyed my place of business and ruined my livelihood.
[[/r d6]]Flaw
1I'll do anything to get my hands on something rare or priceless.
2I'm quick to assume that someone is trying to cheat me.
3No one must ever learn that I once stole money from guild coffers.
4I'm never satisfied with what I have—I always want more.
5I would kill to acquire a noble title.
6I'm horribly jealous of anyone who can outshine my handiwork. Everywhere I go, I'm surrounded by rivals.

The icon was given to Strahd by the archpriest Ciril Romulich, an old family friend, to consecrate the castle and its chapel.

While within 30 feet of the icon, a creature is under the effect of a @spell[protection from evil and good] spell against fiends and undead. Only a creature attuned to the icon can use its other properties.

Augury.

You can use an action to cast an @spell[augury] spell from the icon, with no material components required. Once used, this property can't be used again until the next dawn.

Bane of the Undead.

You can use the icon as a holy symbol while using the Turn Undead or Turn the Unholy feature. If you do so, increase the save DC by 2.

Cure Wounds.

While holding the icon, you can take an action to heal one creature that you can see within 30 feet of you. The target regains [[/r 3d8 + 3]] hit points, unless it is an undead, a construct, or a fiend. Once used, this property can't be used again until the next dawn.
Harvesting valuable materials from corpses.
Looting valuables from corpses.

Roll [[/r 2d4]] when you drink this potion. If you roll the same number on both d4s, nothing happens. Otherwise, you regain hit points equal to the result of the roll + 2. When agitated, silty particles swirl in the potion's murky reddish-brown liquid.

One notable remnant from Waluigi’s destroyed airship is the Warped Gamma Propeller, a massive, twisted propeller blade that once powered the vessel’s erratic flight. This oversized component, roughly 10 feet in diameter, is crafted from a patchwork of blackened steel and purple-painted wood, with jagged edges that suggest it was hastily repaired multiple times. The propeller’s hub is embossed with a bold, yellow “Γ” (the gamma symbol from Waluigi’s hat), slightly dented from the airship’s final crash.

The Warped Gamma Propeller was mounted on the airship’s stern, driving it through the skies with a wobbly, unpredictable motion that matched Waluigi’s chaotic piloting style. Its blades are uneven, with one noticeably bent at a 30-degree angle, causing the airship to lurch and spin during flight—perfect for disorienting enemies but disastrous for stability. Scorch marks and embedded Bullet Bill fragments hint at its exposure to the airship’s own misfired weaponry, likely a result of Waluigi’s penchant for “tricky” battle tactics gone wrong.

When the airship went down (possibly due to a failed scheme involving Wario and a stolen Power Star), the propeller was flung free, landing in a crumpled heap amidst the wreckage. Despite its damage, it still hums faintly with residual energy, suggesting it was powered by some dubious, possibly Toad-engineered tech. The propeller’s surface is scratched with taunting graffiti, like “Waluigi #1!” and “Luigi Stinks!”, reflecting Waluigi’s spiteful rivalry. If salvaged, it could theoretically be repurposed, but its warped shape makes it more a trophy of Waluigi’s failed ambitions than a functional component.

Subtype: Trinket

Description (Player Facing): A Strange Gold Egg
Nestled within the jagged remains of a cracked-open golden dragon egg lies an unusual trinket: a shimmering gold coin, its surface etched with faint, scale-like patterns that mirror the egg’s exterior. The egg itself is a marvel, its golden shell fractured to reveal a molten glow within, as if it once held a fiery essence. The coin, however, feels oddly heavy for its size, and a subtle, almost imperceptible ticking hums from its core—a bomb cunningly disguised as treasure.

Features (GM Facing):
At the end of a long or short rest, the holder of this coin magically loses one gold coin from their inventory, as the trinket siphons wealth to fuel its hidden mechanism. A Passive Perception of 18 is required to notice that this coin differs from others—its weight is slightly off, and the scale-like etchings occasionally pulse with a faint, fiery light. If the bomb is triggered (whether by tampering, a failed investigation check, or a specific in-game condition like extreme heat), it detonates, dealing 3d6 fire damage in a 10-foot radius (Dexterity DC 15 save for half). The coin is destroyed in the explosion, leaving behind charred fragments of the golden egg shell.

You move like the wind, striking faster than your foes can see. You gain the following benefits:

  • Increase your Strength, Dexterity, or Constitution by 1, to a maximum of 20.
  • Ability Score Increase. Increase your Strength, Dexterity, or Constitution score by 1, to a maximum of 20.
  • Battlefield Dancer. Each time you hit a creature, your movement speed increases by 5 feet until the end of your turn. If you attack and hit a creature with a melee weapon attack, you can pass through its space, treating it as difficult terrain.
  • Gain the Slashing Dash special attack (below)

Slashing Dash. Active Ability (Attack)

When you take the @action[Attack] action on your turn, you can replace one of your attacks with a rapid burst of movement, moving up to 30 feet along any surface in a straight line.

You can move on vertical or horizontal surfaces with this movement, can pass through creatures, and do not provoke attacks of opportunity, but cannot pass through objects or terrain. If you are carrying a weapon you are proficient with when you take this action, each time you pass through a creature, it must make a Dexterity saving throw. A creature takes [[/damage 2d6]] + your Strength or Dexterity modifier (your choice) damage of your weapon type on a failed save, or half as much on a successful save. The number of d6 increases by one when your proficiency bonus increases (with the total number of d6 equaling your proficiency bonus).

Once you use this feature, you cannot use it again until you complete a short or long rest.

4th-level fighter @variantrule[optional class features|tce|optional feature]

Whenever you reach a level in this class that grants the Ability Score Improvement feature, you can do one of the following, as you shift the focus of your martial practice:

  • Replace a fighting style you know with another fighting style available to fighters.
  • If you know any maneuvers from the @class[fighter|phb|Battle Master|Battle Master|phb|2-0] archetype, you can replace one maneuver you know with a different maneuver.

A big, weird mushroom gathered from one of numerous places in the faerie manor. There's no telling how it'll taste or what it'll do if ingested.

When consumed either raw or as an ingredient in something it has a random effect from the @UUID[RollTable.f0q96i9Hwm61GDf0] table. The effect lasts for 2d4 hours.

If removed from the faerie plane these mushrooms immediately turn into mundane mushrooms with no special effects.

Beginning at 5th level, you can attack twice, instead of once, whenever you take the @action[Attack] action on your turn.

The number of attacks increases to three when you reach 11th level in this class and to four when you reach 20th level in this class.

Potion, Uncommon

When you drink this potion, you gain the "enlarge" effect of the @UUID[Compendium.dnd5e.spells24.Item.phbsplEnlargeRed]{Enlarge/Reduce} spell for 10 minutes (no Concentration required).

The red in the potion's liquid continuously expands from a tiny bead to color the clear liquid around it and then contracts. Shaking the bottle fails to interrupt this process.

For the duration, the spell enlarges or reduces a creature or an object you can see within range (see the chosen effect below). A targeted object must be neither worn nor carried. If the target is an unwilling creature, it can make a Constitution saving throw. On a successful save, the spell has no effect.

Everything that a targeted creature is wearing and carrying changes size with it. Any item it drops returns to normal size at once. A thrown weapon or piece of ammunition returns to normal size immediately after it hits or misses a target.

Enlarge. The target's size increases by one category—from Medium to Large, for example. The target also has Advantage on Strength checks and Strength saving throws. The target's attacks with its enlarged weapons or Unarmed Strikes deal an extra 1d4 damage on a hit.

Reduce. The target's size decreases by one category—from Medium to Small, for example. The target also has Disadvantage on Strength checks and Strength saving throws. The target's attacks with its reduced weapons or Unarmed Strikes deal 1d4 less damage on a hit (this can't reduce the damage below 1).

Samurai

The Samurai is a fighter who draws on an implacable fighting spirit to overcome enemies. A Samurai's resolve is nearly unbreakable, and the enemies in a Samurai's path have two choices: yield or die fighting.

Bonus Proficiency

When you choose this archetype at 3rd level, you gain proficiency in one of the following skills of your choice: &Reference[skill=History], &Reference[skill=Insight], &Reference[skill=Performance], or &Reference[skill=Persuasion]. Alternatively, you learn one language of your choice.

Fighting Spirit

Starting at 3rd level, your intensity in battle can shield you and help you strike true. As a bonus action on your turn, you can give yourself advantage on weapon attack rolls until the end of the current turn. When you do so, you also gain 5 temporary hit points. The number of temporary hit points increases when you reach certain levels in this class, increasing to 10 at 10th level and 15 at 15th level.

You can use this feature three times, and you regain all expended uses of it when you finish a long rest.

Elegant Courtier

Starting at 7th level, your discipline and attention to detail allow you to excel in social situations. Whenever you make a Charisma (&Reference[skill=Persuasion]) check, you gain a bonus to the check equal to your Wisdom modifier.

Your self-control also causes you to gain proficiency in Wisdom saving throws. If you already have this proficiency, you instead gain proficiency in Intelligence or Charisma saving throws (your choice).

Tireless Spirit

Starting at 10th level, when you roll initiative and have no uses of Fighting Spirit remaining, you regain one use.

Rapid Strike

Starting at 15th level, you learn to trade accuracy for swift strikes. If you take the @action[Attack] action on your turn and have advantage on an attack roll against one of the targets, you can forgo the advantage for that roll to make an additional weapon attack against that target, as part of the same action. You can do so no more than once per turn.

Strength before Death

Starting at 18th level, your fighting spirit can delay the grasp of death. If you take damage that reduces you to 0 hit points and doesn't kill you outright, you can use your reaction to delay falling &Reference[condition=unconscious], and you can immediately take an extra turn, interrupting the current turn. While you have 0 hit points during that extra turn, taking damage causes death saving throw failures as normal, and three death saving throw failures can still kill you. When the extra turn ends, you fall &Reference[condition=unconscious] if you still have 0 hit points.

Once you use this feature, you can't use it again until you finish a long rest.

You have honed your martial prowess and gain a Fighting Style feat of your choice. @feat[Defense|XPHB] is recommended.

Whenever you gain a Fighter level, you can replace the feat you chose with a different Fighting Style feat.

You have a limited well of physical and mental stamina that you can draw on. As a @variantrule[Bonus Action|XPHB], you can use it to regain @variantrule[Hit Points|XPHB] equal to [[/r 1d10]] plus your Fighter level.

You can use this feature twice. You regain one expended use when you finish a @variantrule[Short Rest|XPHB], and you regain all expended uses when you finish a @variantrule[Long Rest|XPHB].

When you reach certain Fighter levels, you gain more uses of this feature, as shown in the Second Wind column of the Fighter Features table.

Your training with weapons allows you to use the @variantrule[weapon mastery properties|XPHB|mastery properties] of three kinds of Simple or Martial weapons of your choice. Whenever you finish a @variantrule[Long Rest|XPHB], you can practice weapon drills and change one of those weapon choices.

When you reach certain Fighter levels, you gain the ability to use the @variantrule[weapon mastery properties|XPHB|mastery properties] of more kinds of weapons, as shown in the @variantrule[Weapon|XPHB] Mastery column of the Fighter Features table.

Fighting Style Feat (Prerequisite: Fighting Style Feature)

When you roll damage for an attack you make with a Melee weapon that you are holding with two hands, you can treat any 1 or 2 on a damage die as a 3. The weapon must have the Two-Handed or Versatile property to gain this benefit.

Variant: Spell Points

Source: Dungeon Masters Guide

With this variant system, a character who has the Spellcasting feature uses spell points instead spell slots to fuel spells. Spell points give a caster more flexibility, at the cost of greater complexity.

In this variant, each spell has a point cost based on its level. The Spell Point Cost table summarizes the cost in spell points of slots from 1st to 9th level. Cantrips don't require slots and therefore don't require spell points.

Instead of gaining a number of spell slots to cast your spells from the Spellcasting feature, you gain a pool of spell points instead. You expend a number of spell points to create a spell slot of a given level, and then use that slot to cast a spell. You can't reduce your spell points total to less than 0, and you regain all spent spell points when you finish a long rest.

Spells of 6th level and higher are particularly taxing to cast. You can use spell points to create one slot of each level of 6th or higher. You can't create another slot of the same level until you finish a long rest.

The number of spell points you have to spend is based on your level as a spellcaster, as shown in the Spell Points by Level table. Your level also determines the maximum-level spell slot you can create. Even though you might have enough points to create a slot above this maximum, you can't do so.

The Spell Points by Level table applies to bards, clerics, druids, sorcerers, and wizards. For a paladin or ranger, halve the character's level in that class and then consult the table. For a fighter (Eldritch Knight) or rogue (Arcane Trickster), divide the character's level in that class by three. 

For an Artificer, add half your levels (rounded up) in the artificer class to to determine your available spell points. (homebrew)

This sturdy tankard contains a funky and earthy ale that has a savory quality to it. Like drinking a delicious broth. While it is a bit like a dark ale mixed with dried mushrooms, it's got a nice punch, and would make a filling stand-in for a meal.

Effect: Drinking just one full mug of this strange brew counts as having eaten a full package of rations. However, it also inflicts an effect from the @UUID[RollTable.f0q96i9Hwm61GDf0] table which lasts for one hour.

These arrows appear to be plants plucked from the earth, their fletching is actually delicate petals, their shafts are woody stalks, and instead of arrowheads they have knots of gnarled roots. These arrows deal bludgeoning damage instead of piercing.

If the arrow strikes a flat surface a 10ft circular patch of soft, noise muffling moss quickly grows around the impact point. Walking on this moss makes no sound, and gives advantage of stealth checks made to move quietly in that area.

Other Projectiles: These can be acquired as crossbow bolts, and the root heads can be removed to function as sling bullets, if desired.

As an action, you can splash the contents of this vial onto a creature within 5 feet of you or throw the vial up to 20 feet, shattering it on impact. In either case, make a ranged attack against a creature or object, treating the acid as an improvised weapon. On a hit, the target takes 2d6 acid damage.
A creature that drinks this vial of liquid gains advantage on saving throws against poison for 1 hour. It confers no benefit to undead or constructs.

This small decorated shot glass contains a swig of something stronger. A powerful shot of a faerie alcohol is contained within.

Effect: Each time you drink this you gain [[/r 1d4]] temporary hit points. Drinking additional shots increases the temporary hit gain by an additional d4 for each shot of this alcohol you've already consumed that day.

These temporary hit points follow all standard temporary hit point rules, and are not cumulative.

You can safely consume a number of these shots up to your Constitution modifier. After that, each time you take another shot you gain the poisoned condition for 1 hour (even if normally immune) and must make a DC 20 Constitution saving throw to avoid taking (2) 1d4 acid damage for every shot you've consumed that day.

A singe serving of high-end fey brandy, it smells of peaches, fig, and apples.

Effect: Upon drinking this brandy a creature must make a successful DC 16 Constitution save against a magical sleep effect. On success the creature gains a level of exhaustion but remains awake, on failure they immediately fall asleep for 1d8 hours.

If woken up from this sleep they instead gain an exhaustion level. If left alone they will sleep until the alcohol runs its course, and awake rested and feeling fresh.

This can effect creatures usually immune to sleep or incapable of sleeping.

A huge fig-like fruit plucked from the tree growing in the foyer of the Faerie manor. It is fragrant and probably delicious.

Once eaten, you discover that you can read and speak fluent Sylvan for 1 hour.

This long, two-handed weapon is light, the staff portion made of a flexible, woody stem. It is topped with a large flower bud of densely packed petals that are sturdy enough to serve as a bludgeon.

In its default state it deals bludgeoning damage. When this weapon is exposed to daylight (natural or magical) the flower bud blooms, revealing a blade of milky gray steel which is wickedly sharp, and remains open for the rest of the day. The Morning Glory closes itself again when night falls or it spends at least an hour in darkness.

This goblet or cup holds a single serving of red, red wine. It smells sweet as strawberries and potent alcohol.

Any creature drinking this wine must make a DC 15 Constitution saving through or suffer the poisoned condition for an hour. The potent fey magic in the wine ignores immunity.

While the creature remains poisoned they also gain proficiency in performance, as well as half proficiency in any musical instrument they pick up. If they are already proficient they gain expertise instead, and if they have expertise they instead gain advantage on any related checks.

Once the wine wears off the creature gains a level of exhaustion and loses all benefits the wine provided.

Uncommon Consumable. A bottle of extraordinarily expensive wine looted from one of the vampire dinner parties at Raventree Manor during the dimensional chaos of Highsun 16-22, 1040 BF. The label identifies it as a vintage from 687 BF (268 years old), produced in vineyards that no longer exist, from grapes cultivated by vampire lords who appreciated fine wine almost as much as fine blood. The bottle itself is a work of art—hand-blown glass with intricate etchings, sealed with wax bearing the crest of House Raventree.

When you consume this wine (drinking the full bottle takes 1 minute), you gain the following benefits for 1 hour:

  • +2 bonus to Charisma (Persuasion) and Charisma (Deception) checks (the wine's sophistication rubs off on you, somehow)
  • Advantage on saving throws against poison and disease
  • You regain 3d8 + 3 hit points as the enchanted vintage courses through your system
  • You gain darkvision out to 60 feet (if you already have darkvision, its range increases by 30 feet)
  • Your blood becomes mildly toxic to vampires for the duration—any vampire that bites you takes 2d6 necrotic damage as the enchanted wine reacts violently to their digestive process

However, the wine is also strongly associated with vampire magic. For the duration of the effect, you are treated as an undead creature for purposes of spells and effects that specifically target undead (such as Turn Undead, though you're not actually compelled to flee). This is usually not a problem for Wario, who uses the wine purely for its healing and social benefits, but it has caused awkward moments when he's been suddenly affected by a paladin's Turn Undead while trying to negotiate a deal.

Wario has approximately 8 bottles of this wine stolen from Raventree Manor's wine cellars (he would have taken more but they were heavy and he was in a hurry). He treats them as both emergency healing potions and luxury items he can sell to collectors for outrageous prices. He's already sold three bottles for 500-750gp each to merchants who didn't ask questions about provenance, and he's considering raising his prices because "clearly I'm undervaluing rare vintage vampire wine."

The wine actually tastes incredible—rich, complex, with notes of ancient oak, dark fruit, and something faintly metallic that's probably the lingering essence of the vampire blood magic used in its creation. Wario doesn't particularly appreciate fine wine (he drinks it like grape juice), but he recognizes quality when it's profitable.
description.chat: You pop the cork with your teeth—you have absolutely no respect for proper wine-opening etiquette—spit it aside, and take a long swig directly from the bottle. The wine is rich, complex, centuries of careful aging creating flavors you can't quite identify but definitely appreciate on a "this tastes expensive" level. You wipe your mouth with the back of your glove, leaving a purple-red stain. "Good stuff! WAH HA HA!" You take another swig. This is too valuable to waste on savoring, better drink it all now before someone tries to take it.

unidentified.name: Ancient Vintage Wine
unidentified.description: A bottle of extremely old wine with an ornate label in archaic script identifying it as a vintage from 687 BF. The bottle itself is beautiful hand-blown glass with intricate etchings, and the wax seal bears the crest of a noble house. The whole thing is covered in dust and decorative spiderwebs. This is clearly valuable, both as a collector's item and as a consumable of significant magical potency.

If woken up from this sleep they instead gain an exhaustion level. If left alone they will sleep until the alcohol runs its course, and awake rested and feeling fresh.

This can effect creatures usually immune to sleep or incapable of sleeping.

A dusty bottle of wine stolen from the cellars of the Feywild Manor during the 'Satyr Eviction' (Day 25). The liquid inside shifts color from green to purple.

Effect: Consuming this wine acts as a Potion of Heroism (10 Temp HP, Bless effect), but for the next hour, the drinker cannot speak without rhyming. Failing to rhyme causes 1d4 psychic damage.
description.chat: Waluigi uncorks the bottle with his teeth. 'Time for a drink, to help me think!'

description.value:
This bright red apple appears entirely harmless, and to the untrained eye there is nothing amiss about it. However, those that have glimpsed it's magical nature know that it harbors a dangerous poison.

Eating this entire apple would deal (42) 12d6 poison damage to the creature that did, and provides no nutrition whatsoever.

This apple can be divided up, which causes the damage to be divided among the pieces. A single slice of apple deals 1d6 poison damage, while half an apple would deal 6d6 poison damage, and so forth.
A slim iron key they probably unlocked a cabinet, chest, or something similar.

A trio of orange crystals that gleam with faerie energy and looks like a perpetual sunset. Touching them makes the fingertips tingle when, and imparts a lightheaded sensation not unlike being inebriated while they are held.

Rare Item (Authenticity Questionable). A stained piece of parchment covered in recipe instructions, measurements, and what appear to be flour handprints. Wario claims this is the original, authentic recipe for Princess Peach's legendary cake—the cake that was so delicious it became famous throughout the Mushroom Kingdom before the war, served at royal functions, and considered one of the great culinary achievements of the pre-war era.

The recipe is written in elegant script (too elegant to be Wario's handwriting), with detailed instructions for a multi-layered strawberry cake with cream filling and decorative frosting. The measurements are in pre-war Mushroom Kingdom units, and there are marginal notes like "His Majesty preferred extra strawberries" and "Princess requests heart-shaped decoration for festivals."

The parchment shows significant age—yellowed edges, small tears, stains from what might be actual cake ingredients (or might just be random kitchen spills from whoever actually wrote this). There's a royal seal watermark visible when held up to light, which Wario points to as "proof of authenticity."

If the recipe is actually followed: Make an Intelligence check (using Cook's Utensils proficiency if you have it). On a 15 or higher, you successfully create a cake that is genuinely delicious—anyone who eats a slice regains 2d4+2 hit points and gains advantage on Charisma checks for 1 hour as they're put in a wonderful mood by the exceptional taste. On a 10-14, you create a good but not spectacular cake that provides the healing but not the Charisma bonus. On a 9 or lower, something goes wrong and you waste the ingredients.

The Authenticity Question: Wario acquired this recipe during a looting expedition to the ruins of Peach's castle sometime around 1005 BF. He claims he found it in the royal kitchens, sealed in a waterproof container, preserved perfectly for exactly this purpose. Skeptics point out that:

  • The parchment's age is inconsistent—it looks old, but not 85+ years old
  • The royal seal watermark matches Peach-era documentation, but Wario could have stolen blank royal stationery and written this himself
  • Several ingredients listed didn't become available in the Mushroom Kingdom until after Peach's death, suggesting the recipe was written later
  • Wario has been caught selling "authentic royal recipes" before, most notably "Bowser's Secret Fire Flower Chili Recipe" which turned out to be copied from a common cookbook with "add more heat" scribbled in the margins

Wario refuses to address these inconsistencies, insisting the recipe is genuine and pricing it at 5,000 gold pieces for interested buyers ("It's a piece of history! Priceless! I'm practically giving it away at 5,000!"). He's also created multiple "certified copies" that he sells for 500 gold pieces each, claiming they're "authorized reproductions" (they're just transcriptions he made himself).

The truth is ambiguous: the recipe might be authentic, might be a skilled forgery, or might be a real recipe that Wario found and is now wildly exaggerating the provenance of. The cake it produces is genuinely good regardless of authenticity, which Wario considers the only fact that matters ("Does it matter WHERE the recipe came from if the cake tastes amazing? No! Stop asking questions and pay me!").
description.chat: You carefully unfold the parchment, treating it with exaggerated reverence as if it's a sacred relic. "Behold! The ORIGINAL recipe for Princess Peach's legendary cake! Used at royal banquets! Tasted by kings! Queens! That plumber guy!" You point at the flour handprints with pride. "See? These are probably Peach's ACTUAL handprints! Priceless! Historical artifact! You can't put a price on history! But if you could, it would be 5,000 gold pieces! Final offer! Non-negotiable!" You're already mentally spending the money before they've even agreed to buy it.

description.value:
This wooden weapon is sprouted from a roughly fistsized seed that's still attached to its base. A large, red thorn creates the weapon's pointed tip. Dense, thorny vines coil around the top and bottom of the haft, with small, glowing splits appearing in the wood beneath them. You gain a +1 bonus to attack and damage rolls made with this magic weapon.

In addition, this weapon has 5 charges and regains all expended charges daily at dawn. When you make a ranged attack with the weapon, you can choose to expend 1 of its charges. Hit or miss, the weapon explodes into thorny shrapnel after it reaches the target. The target and each creature within 10 feet of it must make a DC 15 Dexterity saving throw. A creatures takes [[/damage 1d8 type=piercing]] damage on a failed save, or half as much damage on a successful one. If the target was hit by the attack, it automatically fails the saving throw. Immediately after the weapon explodes, the seed reappears at your location and regrows the weapon into your hand.

Recovered from the false Lady Aurelian — the Feyward manor’s overgrowth wearing its owner’s face — who cheerfully admitted she struck the real Aurelian in the stomach mid-flight and trapped her in the ring.   • Band engraved ‘OC’ — the same initials carved into Corvinarus bedframes.

A signet ring found in the grass on a table in Lady Aurelian’s dark bedroom and recognised by Hjumpik on sight. It can create and destroy connections between the fractured manors: it can speed the ritual of opening the portal, or sever the link entirely. In Hjumpik’s pocket since ~19 Harvestide, 1040 BF (Feyward time).

  • Creates or destroys connections between the manors — a key that can lock and unlock doors, install new ones and take old ones off their frames.
  • Can accelerate the portal-opening ritual, or sever the connection outright.
  • The Book of Revised History, found the same hour, warns the manors must not be combined while a star shard is in play; the ring can honour that warning or ignore it.
  • Not the OC Soul Ring — that one came off the false Lady’s finger four nights later and is a different object.

Obtained: Hjumpik bumped into a table in the dark, squished something that smelled strong, reached into the grass and found the ring under it.

On the record: in Hjumpik’s pocket — merge or sever, undecided.

The ring does not have an opinion about which function is correct. The question is not what the ring can do. The question is who gets to decide what the ring does. — W.

description.value:
A book Hjumpik picked out of the vegetation by the couch in Aurelian’s rooms and pocketed like a receipt from a shop. It records Raventree Manor in the 980s BF as a thriving academic centre where Toads, orcs and lightning professors exchanged ideas freely, a proto-Liberated Toads movement there ‘enlightened’ by the Iron Legion and then the Mages Guild, and a warning that the manors must not be combined while a star shard is in play.

  • Raventree in the 980s BF was a school, not a horror: Toads, orcs and lightning professors in free exchange.
  • A proto-Liberated Toads movement at Raventree was ‘enlightened’ — suppressed — by the Iron Legion and then the Mages Guild, sixty years before Order 120.
  • The manors must NOT be combined while a star shard is in play; the Oracle’s plan requires exactly that.
  • Hjumpik’s level of engagement on reading it: background lore. Waluigi’s: among the most important intelligence of the Feyward campaign.

Obtained: Resting on or near the couch, partly buried in leaves, not destroyed; Hjumpik identified it, examined it, handed it to Waluigi to read, and put it in his pocket.

On the record: pocketed like a receipt; read in full by Waluigi.

My colleagues have a persistent, infuriating habit of finding historically critical documents and treating them like grocery lists. — W.

A card to Woodfellow’s library in the Feyward manor, given to Hjumpik by the goblin patron Artameer Fellow during the Revel crisis (~18 Harvestide, 1040 BF). Woodfellow issues cards only to people he assesses as genuinely knowledgeable; the return policy is one week, or the borrower becomes a book.

  • Access to Woodfellow’s library and its rare fey texts.
  • One week to return a book, or the borrower becomes a book. Woodfellow is equanimous about this.
  • Issued on an assessment of knowledge — a credential with actual standards, which Waluigi notes was not extended to Waluigi.

Obtained: Given to Hjumpik in the library after he found ‘Concerning the Nature and Sustenance of Revels Eternal’; Artameer Fellow is the patron whose previous card Wario stole to check out the Feyward Book of Many Things.

On the record: received from Artameer Fellow; nothing borrowed on it yet.

The transformation-as-late-fee system is the most effective library enforcement mechanism Waluigi has encountered in any documented plane. — W.

The housebound can move through a space as narrow as 1 inch wide without squeezing. It is also immune to being restrained or grappled.

The housebound can move through objects as if they were difficult terrain.

The housebound can perfectly meld with any medium sized inanimate object, or within walls. The only requirement is that the wall space be in dim light or darkness when they enter.

While merged with this object they cannot be detected with normal senses. The Housebound can remain on that surface as long as they want, and can move along it to any connected surfaces or objects large enough to hold them.

The housebound can hide invisibly on the surface of most objects.
While in sunlight, the housebound has disadvantage on attack rolls, ability checks, and saving throws.

Melee Weapon Attack: +5 to hit, 5 ft., one creature. Hit: 10 (2d6 + 3) slashing damage.

The housebound attacks with its shadowy claws, rending flesh with horrible ease.
In the first round of a combat, the Housebound has advantage on attack rolls against any creature it has surprised.

The Housebound is visible if its reflection can be seen in a mirror or other reflective surface. The Housebound appears as a monochromatically skinned bipedal humanoid with an interlaced web of scars covering its flesh.

Fawful's Forces packet sheet — Hypno-Helm. Built by tools/build-forge-packets.py from the NPC Forge roster data/forge/fawfuls-forces.json (entry hypno-helm): Tiny construct (Fawful-Bot), Unaligned; CR 2 (proficiency +2, to hit +5 with DEX); AC 14 (helmet shell), hit points 36 (8d4+16), speed 30 ft., climb 30 ft.. A GM scene kit for the Fawful's Forces article's present (1040 BF), not a filed event; the faction article stays the authority.

The helm is the same make as the one Fawful's double wore at Bowser's Castle in 1035 BF, miniaturised and given legs. The faction article lists the occupation's second verb as "mutate"; this is the first — a crawling helmet that hunts a head, clamps on, and starts giving orders in Fawful's voice. The Vat-Warped Thralls in the Bean Garrison folder are what a Hypno-Helm looks like a month later.

Expect it to go for the party's biggest hitter. The host's friends have three choices: knock the helm off (an action, Athletics), hit it off (attacks that miss narrowly hit the friend), or knock the friend out of the fight until the save sticks. Tearing it off hurts; leaving it on hurts more.

Role: controller · tier: Fawful-Bot · folder: Fawful's Furious Freaks / Machines of Fury.

Art

Token plate portraits/fawfuls-forces/hypno-helm.png — NPC Forge render, seed 410004, cut from a flat #FF00FF field. Prompt: Clean cel-shaded cartoon character art in the style of Mario & Luigi RPG concept art, bold dark outlines, flat colours, simple shading. A green dome-shaped robotic helmet with a glowing hypnotic spiral visor on the front, a brass funnel on top, a thin antenna with a red bulb, walking on four thin brass spider legs with little claws. Full body, whole figure visible, three-quarter view, centred, isolated on a plain flat solid magenta background (#FF00FF), no floor, no ground shadow, no text, no border.

languages.custom: speaks Beanish and Common in Fawful's voice

description.value: Melee Weapon Attack: reach 5 ft., one Medium or smaller creature. Hit: 1d4 + 3 bludgeoning damage and the helm clamps onto the target's head. The target must succeed on a DC 13 Wisdom saving throw (with advantage if it is already wearing a helmet) or be charmed by the helm while it is attached (see Fawful's Voice). The helm can be attached to only one creature at a time.

Recharge 5–6. The visor spins. Each creature within 15 feet of the helm that can see it must succeed on a DC 13 Wisdom saving throw or be incapacitated until the end of its next turn, giggling helplessly. A creature that is charmed by a Hypno-Helm automatically fails.

A creature the helm is attached to and has charmed hears Fawful's voice in its own head. At the start of each of the host's turns the helm chooses how the host moves and what action it takes (the host can't take bonus actions or reactions the helm doesn't ask for). The host can repeat the DC 13 Wisdom saving throw at the end of each of its turns; on a success it is no longer charmed until the end of its next turn, but the helm stays attached and may try again. A host that takes damage from the helm's side has advantage on its next save.

While attached, the helm moves with the host and has three-quarters cover from everyone but the host. An attack roll against the attached helm that misses by 4 or less hits the host instead. The helm comes off when it drops to 0 hit points or when a creature within 5 feet of the host uses an action to tear it off with a successful DC 13 Strength (Athletics) check (the host can't do this itself while charmed). When it comes off, the host takes 1d6 psychic damage as the swirl stops and is no longer charmed.

Built by tools/build-forge-packets.py from the NPC Forge roster data/forge/fawfuls-forces.json (entry intake-drone): Small construct (Fawful-Bot), Unaligned; CR 1 (proficiency +2, to hit +4 with DEX); AC 13 (brass shell), hit points 27 (6d6+6), speed 10 ft., fly 40 ft. The vacuum intake is the oldest trick in the Beanish playbook — the 1035 BF record has it on the head of Fawful's own double — and the Intake Drone is that trick given rotors. It drifts along the castle's ceilings, hums, and then hauls whatever it fancies ten feet across the floor and into the funnel. The occupation uses them as retrievers: a drone brings the Countess a prisoner the way a dog brings a stick.

Fight it like a grab, not a monster. The pull is the whole statblock; break the grapple, or jam the funnel with a helmet, a chair leg, a Chortle-Bot, and it wheezes and backs off for a turn. Rangers and anyone with a reach weapon do well against them; anyone fighting on a balcony does not.

Role: flying grabber · tier: Fawful-Bot · folder: Fawful's Furious Freaks / Machines of Fury.

The drone points its funnel at one creature it can see within 15 feet. The target must succeed on a DC 12 Strength saving throw or be pulled up to 10 feet straight toward the drone. If the pull ends with the target within 5 feet of the drone, the target is grappled (escape DC 12) — Medium or smaller only — and the drone's Siphon trait applies.

A creature grappled by the Intake Drone takes 1d6 bludgeoning damage at the start of each of the drone's turns as the funnel chews at it, and the drone can fly while carrying a grappled Small or smaller creature.

A creature grappled by the drone, or within 5 feet of its funnel, can use an action to stuff something solid into the intake with a successful DC 12 Dexterity check. The drone takes 2d6 bludgeoning damage, releases anything it is grappling, and can't use Slurp until the end of its next turn.
